title: Adcock posts F.03 fleet video and says Figure plans to keep running the robots
summary: Figure CEO Brett Adcock posted a video captioned 'F.03 humanoid robots' and, asked whether F.03 would be decommissioned once a successor arrives, replied that the plan is to keep running them.
body: Short answer: Figure chief executive Brett Adcock posted a 90-second video on 7 November 2026 captioned simply "F.03 humanoid robots". When a follower asked whether F.03 would eventually be decommissioned as the company works on its next robot, Adcock replied: "The plan is to keep running them, it's quite a good robot."

The question came from an X user who suggested Figure was close to finishing the design of a "Figure 4" and asked whether "Figure 3 eventually be decommissioned, or do you find it too valuable?" Adcock did not confirm anything about a successor's design or timing in his answer. He only addressed the fate of the current fleet.
Why the reply matters

Humanoid makers are iterating quickly, and early buyers and partners want to know whether hardware bought or deployed today will be supported once the next generation arrives. Adcock's answer suggests Figure intends to keep F.03 units in service rather than retire them on a fixed schedule.
What was not said

Adcock gave no numbers for the F.03 fleet, no deployment sites and no timeline for a next-generation robot in these posts. Any claim that a "Figure 4" is near completion comes from the follower's question, not from Figure. HumanoidBeat treats the video post and the reply as the public record.

title: Xinhua and UBTech unveil humanoid robot news anchors Xinyan and Xinyu
summary: Xinhua unveiled two life-size humanoid robot news anchors, Xinyan and Xinyu, built with UBTech and styled by Zhang Yimou, at the World Media Summit in Beijing on 5 November.
body: China's state news agency Xinhua unveiled two humanoid robot news anchors at the World Media Summit in Beijing on 5 November, describing them as the world's first bionic humanoid robot news anchors. That "world's first" label is Xinhua's own claim.
Who built them

The life-size anchors are named Xinyan (female) and Xinyu (male), EastFrontier reported, citing Xinhua. Hong Kong-listed UBTech supplied the technology, from bionic skin, hardware and an operating system to an emotion model and production of the robots. Film director Zhang Yimou was lead image designer, and Xinhua says it fully owns the intellectual property.
Where their words come from

The anchors draw content from Xinhua Yudian, the agency's AI agent for current-affairs news. UBTech chief executive Zhou Jian said the robots pull reviewed information in real time to avoid AI hallucinations. Qian Tong, director of Xinhua's New Media Center, described them as a supporting role in the newsroom that would help with presentation, output in several languages and live interaction.
Demonstration, not deployment

So far the robots have appeared at the summit, where one read news of the forum's opening on stage. Zhou listed possible next settings, including study bases, city reception venues and overseas cultural exchanges, but gave no dates. EastFrontier noted that every account so far originates with Xinhua, so speech quality, latency and cost have not been tested by outside reporters.

title: Embodied AI unveils AIR, a wheeled two-arm robot built to work beside factory staff
summary: Swiss startup Embodied AI unveiled AIR at Humanoid Europe 2026 in Munich, a wheeled robot with light tendon-driven arms that it says can work beside factory staff without a safety cage.
body: Swiss robotics startup Embodied AI unveiled AIR at Humanoid Europe 2026 in Munich on 6 November, a two-armed robot on a wheeled base that it says can work alongside factory staff without a safety cage, according to its announcement and Humanoids Daily.
Light arms, heavy torso

The company calls AIR a humanoid, but it has no legs: it is a torso, two arms and a head on wheels. Embodied AI keeps the motors and other heavy parts in the torso and drives the arms through cables, so the moving parts stay light and give way on contact. A conventional industrial arm is heavy and stiff, which is why it usually sits behind a fence or light curtain. The company has not published AIR's height, weight, reach, battery life or full payload.
Teleoperated first, autonomous later

A remote operator runs AIR from its first shift, and each shift is recorded as training data. The company says the robot takes the task over on its own within about a month. It reports a 95% average task success rate in paid pilots with a consumer electronics maker and an automotive and industrial technology supplier, neither of which it has named, and has not said how success is defined.
Who is behind it

Embodied AI is a 25-person spinout from Swiss university EPFL, based in Lausanne, led by chief executive Francesco Stella. It plans CE marking in 2027, when the EU's new Machinery Regulation takes effect, and says orders open after the Munich show. No price or delivery date has been published, and until it carries the CE mark AIR cannot be sold as a finished machine in the EU.

title: Musk Says Tesla Will Probably Rent Out Optimus Robots Rather Than Sell Them
summary: Elon Musk told Ron Baron that Tesla will probably rent out its Optimus humanoid robots rather than sell them, while discussing manufacturing costs and productivity expectations.
body: Tesla could pursue a rental-based business model for its Optimus humanoid robots rather than selling them directly to customers. Elon Musk discussed the possibility with investor Ron Baron during the 33rd Annual Baron Investment Conference in New York on Friday, November 6.
When Baron asked whether Tesla would rent or sell the robots, Musk responded: "I think probably rent them."
The exchange offers a clearer indication of Tesla's potential commercial approach, although the company has not announced rental prices, contractual terms or a finalized sales policy.
Musk favors renting over direct sales
The discussion took place during a fireside chat between Musk and Baron at the annual investment conference.

Baron asked Musk whether Tesla had decided how it would distribute its humanoid robots commercially. Rather than committing to a direct-sales model, Musk indicated that renting was the more likely option.
The answer suggests Tesla may be considering a recurring-revenue business model for Optimus.

Under such an arrangement, customers could potentially pay to use robots over an agreed period rather than purchasing the machines outright. This could allow Tesla to retain ownership of its hardware while generating ongoing revenue from deployments.
However, Musk did not specify whether the proposed rental approach would apply to all customers or whether Tesla might eventually offer both rental and purchase arrangements.
No rental rate was announced during the conversation. The company has also not disclosed minimum contract lengths, maintenance arrangements, insurance requirements or other commercial terms.
Manufacturing costs could fall toward $20,000
Musk and Baron also discussed the potential manufacturing cost of Optimus.
Baron suggested an initial production cost of approximately $30,000 per robot, potentially declining toward $20,000 over time.
Musk agreed with the figures, responding "Yeah."
Before that exchange, Musk said Optimus would initially cost approximately as much as a car to manufacture, but that production costs should become considerably lower over time.
These figures are manufacturing-cost estimates discussed during the conference, not announced customer prices.
The distinction is particularly important if Tesla chooses to rent the robots. A manufacturing cost of $20,000 or $30,000 does not establish what customers would pay for access to an Optimus unit.
A rental business would also need to account for servicing, repairs, depreciation, logistics and the utilization rate of its robot fleet.
For now, Tesla has not published a commercial pricing structure.
Musk claims robots could outperform human workers
Musk also outlined his expectations for the productivity of humanoid robots.
He argued that a machine capable of operating continuously could generate substantially more weekly output than an ordinary human worker.
During the discussion, Musk suggested that Optimus could eventually achieve approximately five times the weekly productivity of a person.
His reasoning was based on the possibility of operating for 168 hours per week, without the breaks, vacations and other interruptions associated with human labor.

These are Musk's projections rather than independently demonstrated productivity figures. Actual performance will depend on the tasks assigned, reliability, operating costs and the ability of robots to function safely in real working environments.

Nevertheless, the potential economic proposition is significant. If humanoid robots can perform repetitive industrial tasks reliably, businesses could potentially justify recurring payments based on labor savings and increased production.
External deliveries remain a longer-term target
Tesla's commercial ambitions for Optimus are still developing.

According to Not a Tesla App's November 6 reporting, Musk has discussed beginning deliveries to outside companies around the end of 2027. The company intends to deploy robots internally in its own factories before expanding external distribution.
That timeline remains a target rather than a confirmed delivery commitment.

The rental comments also leave important questions unanswered. Tesla has not announced whether customers will be able to purchase Optimus outright, whether rental contracts will be available to smaller businesses or how the company will handle maintenance and technical support.
For now, Musk's remarks provide an indication of Tesla's preferred commercial direction, but not a finalized business model.
If Tesla ultimately retains ownership and rents its humanoid robots to customers, Optimus could become a recurring-revenue business rather than a conventional hardware product.

title: KIST KAPEX humanoid heads toward LG commercialization after science award
summary: KIST’s KAPEX humanoid, built with more than 90% domestically made core parts and able to walk while carrying over 20 kg, has its technology path into LG after Lee Jong-won’s November science award.
body: Short answer: South Korea’s KIST developed the KAPEX AI humanoid with more than 90% locally made core components and transferred core technology to LG Electronics, while group head Lee Jong-won received the November Korea Science and Technology Award for the work, Seoul Economic Daily reported on 4 November 2026.
What KAPEX is claimed to do

Seoul Economic Daily describes KAPEX as a bipedal platform that can walk while carrying loads of more than 20 kilograms, adjust grip strength through fingertip sensors, and combine domestically developed actuators, joints, sensors and control AI. Actuators are said to generate up to 300 newton metres of torque in a package sized for a human joint. Those performance figures are KIST’s claims as reported by the paper, not independent lab verification here.

Lee, head of the Humanoid Research Group at KIST’s AI and Robot Institute, was named November recipient of the Korea Science and Technology Award by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Research Foundation for localising and commercialising those core parts.
LG partnership path

SED says KIST transferred KAPEX core technology to LG Electronics in September 2025. The reported partnership splits roles: LG Electronics on the robot platform, LG AI Research on physical AI, LG Energy Solution on all-solid-state batteries, and Robostar on mass production, with smaller firms and universities also involved. Field testing is planned to expand from a living-lab kitchen and lounge inside KIST into hospitals and public facilities.
Commercialisation caveat

Lee himself told SED that short demonstrations are not the same as months of unsupervised workplace duty, and that judgement, hand dexterity, batteries, durability and safety still need work. For humanoid industry readers, KAPEX is a localisation and technology-transfer story first: a government lab platform moving into a chaebol manufacturing stack, with awards marking research progress rather than a retail product launch date.

title: Hyundai Mobis starts Atlas actuator prototypes at Uiwang
summary: Hyundai Mobis began November prototype production of actuators for Boston Dynamics’ Atlas at its Uiwang research centre, aiming to supply all 31 joints by 2028.
body: Short answer: Hyundai Mobis has begun prototype production of actuators for Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid at its Uiwang research centre in Gyeonggi Province, with a target of supplying all 31 joints per robot by 2028, according to trade coverage dated early November 2026.
What Mobis is building

The Robotics Media reports that November 2026 prototype work covers the motorised joint components that act as Atlas’s muscles. Mobis aims eventually to supply every one of the 31 actuators on a single Atlas unit. The same report says actuators can account for 40% to 60% of a humanoid’s manufacturing cost, which is why an automotive-scale supplier sees the category as strategic.

Hyundai Motor Group owns Boston Dynamics, giving Mobis a captive first customer while it also says it wants to sell components to other humanoid makers. That captive relationship is a competitive fact of group ownership, not a guarantee that Atlas volume will hit every plan.
Factory and earnings backdrop

The Robotics Media says Mobis is planning a US plant with annual capacity of 350,000 actuator units, expandable to 700,000 with a second shift, timed around Atlas’s planned 2028 commercial rollout at Hyundai Motor Group’s Georgia plant. Alongside the robotics push, the outlet cites Q3 2026 operating profit of 914.1 billion won, about $684.7 million, up 17.2% year over year, and R&D spending set to exceed about $1.5 billion annually.
Herald Business and other Korean business wires also covered the November prototype start in the same earnings window. Exact joint specifications and customer pricing are not public in these reports.
How to read the announcement

Prototype production is not volume supply. Mobis still has to clear performance and reliability testing with Boston Dynamics before 2028 shipments. For humanoid watchers, the signal is supply-chain localisation inside the Hyundai group: Atlas’s most expensive bill-of-materials category is being pulled into an auto-parts production system rather than left entirely to specialist robotics vendors.

summary: Figure CEO Brett Adcock posted a new video on X on 6 November 2026 with the caption "One day the entire world will look like this," showing humanoid robots walking through campus and office spaces. Reactions on X were mixed.
body: Short answer: On 6 November 2026, Figure founder and CEO Brett Adcock posted on X a video of humanoid robots walking through campus and office spaces, captioned: "One day the entire world will look like this." The post is a new viral clip and caption, separate from Figure's earlier 2–3 November BotQ campus-walk coverage.

In the 6 November post, Adcock wrote exactly: "One day the entire world will look like this." The attached video (about 86 seconds in the X media metadata) shows white-and-black bipedal humanoids moving through indoor corridors, lobbies and outdoor campus-style walkways. Adcock did not add production rates, delivery totals or customer names in that caption.
How this differs from the earlier BotQ walk clip

HumanoidBeat already covered a late-October/early-November Adcock video of completed Figure 03 units walking away from BotQ (Figure 03 robots leave BotQ on foot, 3 November 2026). That piece stressed the gap between a campus walk and disclosed factory output. This 6 November post is a different clip and a different framing: a short, forward-looking caption rather than a BotQ production claim.
Reach and reaction (as reported on X)

When this story was prepared, X public metrics on Adcock's post showed on the order of about 263,000 impressions, about 3,890 likes, about 624 replies and about 368 reposts. Those counters move quickly and are not independently audited. Public replies quoted in the wider X thread split between enthusiasm for a humanoid-filled workplace future and unease about the same scene; those are user reactions, not company statements.
What the post does not establish

Adcock's caption is a vision line, not a shipment tally. The video does not, by itself, state weekly BotQ output, how many of the robots shown are customer-bound, or whether every segment was fully autonomous. Readers should not treat the clip as proof of mass commercial deployment. For manufacturing context that remains separate from this caption, see our earlier BotQ walk report.
Caveats

Quote and link above are taken from Adcock's public X post. Impression and engagement figures are X platform metrics at scout time, not audited audience research. Scene descriptions summarise what appears in the posted video; they are not a factory tour or an independent product test.

title: Chinese humanoid makers push factory and cafe trials in South Korea
seo_title: Chinese humanoids pursue South Korea factory and cafe trials
summary: UBTech, Unitree, AgiBot and Anyverse Dynamics are pursuing Korean deployments as Seoul expands physical AI funding, according to The Gadgeteer on 6 November 2026.
body: Chinese humanoid robot companies are moving from demos toward factory trials, cafe pilots and paid work in South Korea, The Gadgeteer reported on 6 November 2026.

The report names UBTech Robotics, Unitree Robotics, AgiBot and Beijing startup Anyverse Dynamics as firms working the Korean market. It says Korea has factories and capital, a shrinking workforce, and no domestic humanoid maker shipping robots at the same scale.

According to that report, UBTech says it has sold more than 10,000 robots in South Korea since 2019 across corporate and government customers. Its U1 humanoid is described as about 1.68 metres tall and priced around $25,000. Galaxy Robot Park in Seoul is said to have taken delivery of one after a Shenzhen debut. UBTech is also described as trial ling humanoids on a Korean automotive parts line with Duksan JM Robotics and Ajin Industrial, after adapting hardware for Korea's KC certification.

Anyverse Dynamics is framed as entering through service work. The Gadgeteer says founder Zhang Yufeng previously worked at SK Telecom and Hyundai Motor, and that the company is testing drink service and table clearing with Hollys, starting with a Beijing cafe trial and Korean cafe trials planned for the fourth quarter.

Trade figures in the same article, attributed to Chinese customs data, rank South Korea as China's third largest export market for intelligent bionic robots in the first nine months of 2026, at $20 million, or 9.7 percent of $207 million shipped worldwide. The customs category covers humanoids and robot dogs.

South Korea's government is also described as proposing 3.1 trillion won, about $2.3 billion, for physical AI in its 2027 budget, up from 900 billion won this year, with the bill before the National Assembly. The industry ministry's Manufacturing AI Transformation programme is said to target 500 AI factories by 2030.
Caveats

Figures for sales, prices, budget totals and customs values are as reported by The Gadgeteer citing company statements and Chinese customs data. This article does not independently verify those numbers. Deployment timelines for factory and cafe trials remain company or outlet reported plans.

title: Unitree CEO says GPT-6 powered humanoids painted and played chess with no prior training

summary: South China Morning Post reports Unitree founder Wang Xingxing said at CIIE in Shanghai that the firm's humanoids, powered by OpenAI's GPT-6, painted and played chess without prior training.
body: Short answer: Unitree Robotics founder and CEO Wang Xingxing said at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai that the company's humanoids, powered by OpenAI's GPT-6, can paint pictures and play chess without prior training, according to a South China Morning Post report published on 5 November 2026. The claims are Wang's, as carried by SCMP; this desk has not independently verified a public demo video of those exact tasks.
What Wang said, per SCMP

SCMP writes that Wang spoke on Thursday at CIIE and described Unitree machines executing intricate sequences such as dynamically replacing brush water and blending pigments, guided by realtime model inference. "The precision required to change pigments without error is quite high," Wang said, per the paper. "Seeing it perform at this level with zero training was truly stunning."

The same article says Wang argued the industry's biggest remaining hurdle is no longer digital reasoning or planning but closing a "last millimetre" mechanical gap. That framing treats model side planning as largely solved in his view, and hardware precision as the bottleneck.
How to attribute this

Treat every capability claim here as a CEO statement reported by SCMP, not as a third party lab result. SCMP does not, in the text reviewed, publish a controlled benchmark score or an outside auditor's confirmation. OpenAI's own GPT-6 Cyber materials are about security research agents and are a separate product thread; Wang's remarks concern Unitree robots said to run on GPT-6 for physical tasks.

Until Unitree or OpenAI publish reproducible demos with clear task definitions, the accurate headline is that Wang says GPT-6 powered Unitree humanoids painted and played chess with no prior training, as reported by SCMP from CIIE.

title: Agility's S-4 and Ars interview put Digit unit economics in the open: $8,500/mo RaaS, $200k buy, BOM path to $30k
seo_title: Agility Digit unit economics: $8.5k RaaS, $200k buy, BOM to $30k
summary: Ars Technica's 5 Nov 2026 report on Agility's Nasdaq debut digs into S-4 unit economics: about $8,500 a month RaaS after ~$25,000 deployment, $200,000 hardware purchase plus software fees, and a BOM path from $150,000 toward $30,000 at 10,000 units a year.
body: Hours after Agility Robotics began trading as AGLT, Ars Technica published a detailed look at the company's S-4 registration statement and an interview with co-founder Jonathan Hurst that puts Digit 5's proposed unit economics in plain numbers. This desk already covered the Nasdaq debut itself; the Ars piece is useful for the pricing and cost path that the listing day press release largely skipped.

Short answer: According to the 4 September S-4 filed with the SEC, which Ars also reviewed, Agility's illustrative robots-as-a-service model charges about $25,000 one-time for delivery and deployment plus a recurring $8,500 a month for software and maintenance. Customers can instead buy the hardware for a one-time $200,000 plus about $20,000 deployment, then pay about $36,000 a year ($3,000 a month) for software and maintenance. Ars says Agility estimates its own annual software-and-maintenance cost at $15,000 per robot and a one-time $15,000 deployment cost to Agility.

On the manufacturing side, the S-4 and Ars put Digit v5's bill of materials at about $150,000 at commercial launch, with targets of about $75,000 at 1,000 robots a year and $30,000 at 10,000 a year, with a useful life of about five years. CFO Michael Beer, in an 6 October investor presentation summarised by Ars, framed subscription as replacing roughly $200,000 in annual labour with about $100,000 in annual robot cost, and ownership as replacing about $1.1 million in labour with about $400,000 in robot cost over five years. Those labour-replacement figures are Agility's illustrations, not audited customer results.

Ars also notes Agility earned $1.8 million in revenue against a $140 million operating loss in 2025, and quotes the S-4 warning that the company expects to keep losing money for the foreseeable future. The subscription revenue maths in the filing, Ars writes, lean on an unidentified customer's $300 million order for 1,000 Digit 5 robots over three years—the S-4 describes it as one customer's commitment to deploy $300 million of Digit v5 over a multi-year period, subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications. Agility's listing-day release cites more than $300 million in committed multi-year Digit 5 orders on the same conditions.

Hurst told Ars that RaaS lowers customer risk because the monthly rate is "comparable to the human labor rate," and that Digit 5 is aimed at structured workplaces, not homes. Nyobolt's fast-charge pack is described as delivering 90 minutes of runtime from a nine-minute charge under an exclusive humanoid chemistry deal. Readers should treat battery, safety and labour-replacement claims as company statements relayed by Ars.

What this adds beyond the debut release is a public price book and cost curve that competitors still mostly keep private. Whether those numbers hold once Digit 5 ships in volume is the open question the S-4 itself flags.
analysis: Opinion: Listing-day headlines sell the ticker; the S-4 numbers sell the hard part—subscription ARPU, BOM scale and years of losses. Treat the $8,500 and $30k BOM targets as planning assumptions until Agility reports repeatable deployments at those rates.

title: Agility begins Nasdaq trading as AGLT, first U.S. pure-play listed humanoid company
seo_title: Agility Nasdaq debut as AGLT, first U.S. pure-play humanoid
summary: Agility Robotics began trading on Nasdaq as AGLT on 5 Nov 2026 after closing its Churchill Capital Corp XI deal, calling itself the first U.S. publicly listed pure-play humanoid robotics company.
body: Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker AGLT on 5 November 2026, describing itself as the first U.S. publicly listed pure-play humanoid robotics company with active commercial deployments. The company announced the debut on X: "Today, Agility begins trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol AGLT."

Short answer: According to Agility's press release, common stock and warrants trade as AGLT and AGLTW after completion of the previously announced business combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The business combination and related financings represent approximately $465 million in gross capital raised before transaction expenses, the company said. A companion release covers the closing of that combination.

Agility says it enters the public markets with nearly three years of real-world deployment experience, more than 65,000 hours of operation, and more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5, its next-generation humanoid, subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications. Those order and hour figures are the company's own disclosures in the Nasdaq debut release, not independently audited totals published in the sources reviewed here.

Digit is already operating with enterprises including GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, the release states. Agility recently expanded its partnership with GXO to deploy Digit at two additional U.S. logistics facilities in early 2027, building on a Georgia site where Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes, according to the same announcement. The company's growing customer base also includes AGCO under a commercial agreement described in the debut release. CEO Peggy Johnson said becoming public gives Agility access to more resources to accelerate workplace deployments of robots that take on repetitive, physically demanding tasks.

Digit 5 is presented as a cooperatively safe platform intended to work closer to people than earlier generations, supported by Agility's robotics stack, safety systems and the Agility Arc enterprise software platform. The release frames that software and safety layer as part of how Agility plans to scale deployments, not merely as a hardware refresh. Readers should treat product-roadmap language as forward-looking statements from the company.

The "first U.S. publicly listed pure-play humanoid" claim is Agility's characterisation of its listing. It does not mean Agility is the only company working on humanoids, nor that every peer is private; it means Agility presents AGLT as a pure-play humanoid listing with commercial Digit work already under way. Other robotics or automation firms may trade publicly with broader product mixes; Agility's point is the pure-play humanoid framing plus live customer sites.

Investors should read the full SEC and company filings for risks, dilution, warrant terms (AGLTW) and how much of the roughly $465 million gross capital remains after fees. A listing day is not a revenue forecast. Past tote counts and pilot hours do not assure that Digit 5 multi-year orders will convert on schedule or at the margins Agility needs.

What to watch next is whether Digit 5 orders convert on the stated milestones, whether the additional GXO sites open as described for early 2027, how Toyota and Schaeffler deployments expand, and whether Agility publishes clearer unit economics once it reports as a public company.
analysis: Opinion: A Nasdaq ticker is a financing and visibility event, not proof that humanoid robots are ready for every warehouse. The useful evidence in Agility's own release remains the deployment hours, named customers and conditional Digit 5 orders—figures that still need to be tested against delivery schedules and margins over the next several quarters.

title: RoboColosseum's Opening Results: No AI Policy Completed a Unitree G1 Humanoid Task
seo_title: RoboColosseum: no policy completed a Unitree G1 humanoid task
summary: In RoboColosseum's real-world tests, no evaluated AI policy completed any of five Unitree G1 humanoid tasks, with average progress of 13.3% to 23.2%, its paper says.
body: RoboColosseum, a new open initiative for testing AI models on physical robots, launched on 4 November 2026, and its initial published results show how far humanoids still have to go: none of the evaluated policies completed any of the five tasks set for the Unitree G1 humanoid, according to the project's paper.

The project announced itself on X as "an open robot eval initiative" backed by Hugging Face, BitRobot Network and the Singapore Embodied AI Centre, offering access to more than 100 robots, more than 140 in-the-wild scenes, open rollout data and "10,000 FREE eval hrs". The paper's authors come from NUS, the University of Washington, Stanford, UNC, Ai2, Oxford, Hugging Face, BitRobot and the Singapore Embodied AI Centre.

The paper tested five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four robot bodies: the SO-101 arm, a Franka arm, a Bimanual-YAM setup and the Unitree G1 humanoid. On the G1, no policy finished any of the five tasks, and average task progress ranged from 13.3% to 23.2%. In other words, the systems made partial progress but did not complete the jobs. The result concerns the policies tested, not the limits of the G1 hardware itself.
Unitree said on X it was "great to see Unitree G1s being used as the primary embodiment" in the humanoid benchmark category.

The evaluations ran from 17 September to 28 October 2026 on a fleet of more than 100 robots in the US, UK, Singapore, Malaysia and China. The Open Track gathered 5,699 blinded pairwise comparisons at 124 sites, and a separate Fine-tune Track covered 20 tasks with 100 demonstrations each.

The authors report that frontier AI agents rival specialised VLA policies, but that all approaches struggle on open-world tasks. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 led on the SO-101, while pi0.5 led on the Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Agreement between rankings on different robot bodies was low, with a Kendall's W of 0.24, so a model that does well on one robot may not do well on another.
Ai2 said on X that its MolmoAct 2 placed second, behind GPT-6 Astra, in the Franka arm tests without extra training for those tasks.
Hugging Face, a founding partner, said that "every rollout, failures included" is open on its Hub. The project has pledged the 10,000 free evaluation hours to academic labs.
For humanoid makers, the G1 numbers set a measurable starting point rather than a sign of readiness: getting from partial progress to finished tasks remains the open problem.

title: Samsung's chairman visited the RX robotics office on his fourth anniversary in the role
seo_title: Samsung chairman visits the RX robotics office
summary: Lee Jae-yong visited Samsung's RX robotics office in Seoul on 27 October, his fourth anniversary as chairman, Korean papers report.
body: Short answer: Samsung Electronics chairman Lee Jae-yong visited the company's Robotics eXperience (RX) Business Promotion Office on the afternoon of 27 October 2026, Korean papers report. The date was the fourth anniversary of his becoming chairman, on 27 October 2022. The office is at Samsung's Seoul R&D campus in Umyeon-dong, Seocho-gu, and Maeil Business Newspaper, Businesskorea and SBS each say this was his first visit since the office was created in July.

SBS reported that during the visit he checked development work, including precision manipulation with a humanoid's arms and hands, and that Roh Tae-moon, president and head of the Device eXperience division, was with him. Maeil Business Newspaper reported that he reviewed humanoid technologies that could be shown at CES 2027 in Las Vegas in January. Businesskorea reported that Samsung is reviewing plans to show related technology there. None of the three papers quotes Samsung announcing a CES exhibit. The Hankyoreh had already reported that a visit was expected and that the group is developing tendon-style, five-finger hands; that account is in our earlier report.

Businesskorea and Maeil Business Newspaper describe the RX office as a unit set up in July under Roh Tae-moon to bring together robotics work that had been spread across the company, from strategy to core technology and commercialisation. Maeil Business Newspaper dates it to 21 July. Both papers say Samsung is building a robot data factory at its Gumi plant to collect learning data. Businesskorea and SBS say the company has a goal of turning its plants in Korea and abroad into AI-based autonomous factories by 2030. Those are plans as the papers describe them, not results.

Businesskorea reported that at the Samsung AI Forum last month, Chris Hauser, a lab director in the RX office, said general-purpose robots would need a task success rate of 99.99 percent before they could work in homes or factories. He told the forum, "There is still a long way to go." For the wider market these robots would be walking into, see our report on Chinese humanoid makers seeking trials in South Korea.
analysis: Opinion: Spending an anniversary inside the robotics office shows where the chairman's attention was that day. A site visit is not a product launch. The practical test is whether a hand demonstration becomes a robot that can hold a high success rate on a real line, which Samsung's own lab director has described as still ahead.
disclaimer: The visit, the July date and the factory plans are as reported by Maeil Business Newspaper, Businesskorea and SBS. SBS notes that its English article was machine-translated and may contain errors. Samsung has not published its own account of the visit in the sources reviewed here. This is not investment advice.

title: NEURA aims to run five robot gyms by the end of 2026, the New York Times reports
seo_title: NEURA aims for five robot gyms by the end of 2026
summary: The New York Times reports NEURA aims to run five robot gyms by year-end, including one open in Hangzhou, China.
body: Short answer: NEURA Robotics aims to have five robot-training gyms running by the end of 2026, including one already opened in Hangzhou, China, with ten more expected after that, the New York Times reported on 27 October 2026. The Indian Express carried the same report the next day. NEURA's chief told the Times that more than 2,600 applicants have asked for space at one of the sites.

The Times said a reporter was shown the gym NEURA developed with the Technical University of Munich, beside Munich Airport, where as many as 100 humanoid and other robots were training around the clock. In that account the robots picked up car parts, stacked boxes and tightened a grip on a glass as water was added, copying trainers who guided them from a distance. NEURA has signed dozens of automotive, logistics, pharmaceutical and other companies to train there and has not named them, the paper wrote. A skill learned by one robot is meant to reach the others through a shared cloud system. The opening of that gym, and the 4NE1 Gen 4 launch on 22 October, are in our earlier report.

The Times also reported that NEURA is working with Bosch and other companies to put sensor suits on more than 1,000 workers, recording how they move during ordinary shifts. Interact Analysis, a consulting firm, told the paper that more than 90 humanoid data-collection centres are running in China, at least 50 more are under development, and Europe has fewer than 10. "We are not efficient anymore," NEURA founder David Reger told the Times.

The same article says robots are expected to move into production at a BMW site by the first quarter of next year. The paragraph before it describes a pilot by Swiss firm Hexagon Robotics with BMW at a plant in Leipzig, and the production sentence does not name the supplier. The Times also wrote that Agile Robots, in Munich, is working with companies including Google DeepMind, and that the British firm Humanoid aims to place robots in Schaeffler's operations by the end of 2026. Zornitsa Todorova, a researcher at Barclays, told the Times the number of humanoids in use worldwide could rise from 15,000 last year to one million in 2030 if costs fall and rules do not block the way. That is her forecast, not a headcount. The Times reported that NEURA raised as much as $1.4 billion in June, that Tether led the round, and that Nvidia and Amazon were among the backers. NEURA told the paper that part of the sum was tied to milestones it was on track to meet. Related reading: Schaeffler's Taicang line and China's output and standards plans.
analysis: Opinion: A long list of applicants, and a gym already open in Hangzhou, shows interest in training time. It does not show that the robots can hold a factory job. The BMW timing in the Times is easy to over-read, because the paper does not say which company's robots are due on that line.
disclaimer: Gym plans, the applicant figure, the funding amount and the sensor-suit project are NEURA's statements as reported by the New York Times. The China and Europe site counts are Interact Analysis figures cited by the Times. The 2030 number is a forecast from a Barclays researcher. This is not investment advice.

title: What humanoid makers have published about runtime and recharge
seo_title: Published humanoid runtimes and recharge times
summary: Agility says Digit 5 will run 90 minutes and recharge in 9; 1X lists 4 hours for NEO; Unitree lists about 3 hours for the H2.
body: Short answer: Three published humanoid runtimes sit between about 90 minutes and 4 hours on a single charge. Agility Robotics says the Digit 5 battery will run for 90 minutes and recharge in 9 minutes. 1X lists 4 hours for NEO. Unitree lists about 3 hours for the H2. Each figure is the company's own, and none is an independent test of a working shift.

Agility's release of 15 October 2026 says Nyobolt is supplying the Digit 5 pack. The company says 90 minutes of runtime and a 9-minute charge are a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from a 2-to-1 ratio on Digit 4, and that the robot could then do more than 20 hours of work in a 24-hour day. The 20-hour figure is time on shift across repeated charges, not one battery cycle. Agility says early access to Digit 5 with this pack is expected in the first half of 2027, with wider availability over the following six to nine months. Digit 5's onboard computer and Pittsburgh plans are in our earlier report.

On its order page, 1X lists a NEO battery of 842 watt-hours, a runtime of 4 hours and a quick charge of 6 minutes for each hour of runtime. The page says that when NEO needs a charge, it plugs itself in. 1X also lists a purchase price of $20,000 or a subscription of $499 a month, and says US deliveries start in 2026. Those are statements on the product page, not a record of robots already delivered.

Unitree's H2 product page lists battery life of about 3 hours, a 15 amp-hour pack rated at 0.972 kilowatt-hours, and a maximum voltage of 75.6 volts, plus a quick-release battery and a charger. A footnote says the parameters can change with the scenario and the configuration. The same page lists the H2 at $29,900 before tax and shipping. A runtime on a spec sheet does not say whether the robot was walking, carrying a load or standing still. The H2 is the full-size Unitree humanoid in our H2-X coverage.
analysis: Opinion: For a warehouse shift, a short runtime with a fast recharge can cover more of the day than a longer runtime that then sits on a charger. The useful comparison is hours of work in a day, and only Agility has published that kind of number, as a target. Spec-sheet hours will not match a real job until someone logs them there.
disclaimer: Runtimes, charge times, prices and delivery timing are the companies' published figures and targets, not independent measurements. Agility's release describes the Digit 5 numbers as expected performance. This is not a recommendation to buy a robot or any security.

title: NEURA unveils a lighter 4NE1 Gen 4 humanoid as the TUM RoboGym opens near Munich
summary: NEURA says its 4NE1 Gen 4 humanoid is 20% lighter and being readied for series production; it launched at the new TUM RoboGym near Munich Airport.
body: Short answer: NEURA Robotics unveiled 4NE1 Gen 4 on 22 October 2026, a new generation of its humanoid robot that the company says is 20 percent lighter than the previous version and is being prepared for series production. The launch coincided with the opening of the TUM RoboGym, a robot training and research centre near Munich Airport run with the Technical University of Munich (TUM), according to both organisations.

According to NEURA, Gen 4 has a slimmer body covered in a black textile outer skin, upgraded hands for finer gripping, and what the company calls Smart Limbs, with reflexes built into each limb. It runs Neuron AI, which NEURA describes as a Perception-Language-Action model that combines vision, touch, force, sound and the robot's own state; the company's example is sensing whether a fastener has clicked into place. Interesting Engineering reported the same details on 23 October.

NEURA says the RoboGym covers more than 2,300 square metres at the LabCampus site. TUM says around 100 humanoid and service robots will initially learn skills there in 48 training cells, with an early focus on industrial applications and intralogistics, and that the data will flow into a curated cloud data lake for research. According to NEURA, partners from more than ten industries, including automotive, pharmaceuticals, logistics, agriculture and care, have been training workflows at the site since September, on tasks such as handling boxes, filling bottles and loading wooden parts.

The partners describe an initial three-year initiative with a combined investment of about €17 million, of which NEURA says it is contributing about €11 million. NEURA says Munich is the first of a planned network of NEURA Gyms, with more being set up in Europe, the United States and China and another in Germany with RWTH Aachen. The company says the robot was also shown at NVIDIA's GTC event in Berlin, where Agile Robots presented its Agile ONE SN humanoid. The announcements do not give a price or delivery date for 4NE1 Gen 4.
analysis: Opinion: Launching a robot together with a training facility reflects a wider industry view that real-world physical data, not only hardware, is what holds humanoids back. Whether Gen 4's claimed improvements lead to dependable factory work will depend on results from sites like the RoboGym, and none have been published yet.
disclaimer: Specifications, plans and investment figures are NEURA's and TUM's own statements and have not been independently verified. This is not investment advice.

title: Generative Bionics plans a 5,000 m² humanoid training "data factory" in Italy with AMD
summary: Generative Bionics says it will build a three-site Physical AI Data Factory network, starting with a 5,000 m² Italian hub due by Q4 2027, using AMD compute.
body: Short answer: Italian humanoid developer Generative Bionics announced on 21 October 2026 that it plans a network of three "Physical AI Data Factory" sites to train humanoid robots, starting with a 5,000-square-metre hub in Italy that it expects to be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027, with AMD as its AI infrastructure partner, according to the company's press release.

The company says fleets of its GENE.01 humanoid will carry out industrial tasks continuously in reproduced real-world work environments chosen with industrial partners, generating data to train what it calls World Action Models. Each environment will also be rebuilt as a digital twin so tasks can be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, conditions and failure modes, and models trained in simulation will return to the physical robots for validation, a loop Generative Bionics calls real-to-sim-to-real.

According to the release, AMD Helios rack-scale systems will provide the compute for processing physical and synthetic data, training models and running simulations. A second site is planned elsewhere in Europe and a third to serve global markets. Generative Bionics says the first hub will be Europe's largest physical AI training facility for humanoid robots; that is the company's own description. Robotics & Automation News reported the plan on 23 October.

Generative Bionics presents the project as supporting European control over humanoid data, models and know-how. The company says AMD Ventures took part in its €70 million seed round led by CDP Venture Capital, and that AMD compute already runs on board GENE.01. Other developers are also combining real and simulated training, including NEURA with its new TUM RoboGym and Unitree with its Rehearsal project.
analysis: Opinion: Dedicated robot data-collection sites are becoming a common bet among European humanoid developers. The timeline is long, with the first hub not due until late 2027, and the announcement gives no cost figure for the network.
disclaimer: Plans, timelines and the "largest" description are Generative Bionics' own statements and have not been independently verified. Funding details are as stated by the company. This is not investment advice.

title: AiMOGA opens worldwide pre-orders for Mobo, a 0.9 m family companion humanoid
summary: AiMOGA Robotics says it has opened global pre-orders for Mobo, a 0.9-metre home companion humanoid with 22 degrees of freedom; no price was announced.
body: Short answer: AiMOGA Robotics, based in Wuhu, China, said on 22 October 2026 that it has unveiled Mobo, its first consumer family companion humanoid, and opened pre-orders worldwide, according to a company press release. The announcement does not state a price or delivery date.

According to AiMOGA, Mobo is 0.9 metres tall, has 22 degrees of freedom and supports more than 20 languages. The company is aiming it at households: object recognition, questions and answers, storytelling and English practice for children, and conversation and reminders for older family members. AiMOGA says the robot recognises family members using face ID and keeps memories linked to each person.

Mobo runs on MoAgent, which AiMOGA describes as its embodied-intelligence agent, with a "dual-brain" design for planning and fast responses and a world model to check whether tasks have been completed. The company says the robot can handle up to 16 tasks in parallel with an interruption response time under 0.2 seconds, and that eligible data is de-identified on the device before it is used for cloud learning. These figures have not been independently tested.

AiMOGA says more than 10,000 prospective users have shown interest since Mobo's debut at the World Robot Conference in August 2026. More broadly, the company says it has sold more than 3,000 robots across over 60 countries and regions, and plans 300 experience centres worldwide and a robot-leasing brand starting in Wuhu, drawing on the manufacturing and sales resources of carmaker Chery.
analysis: Opinion: Home companion humanoids are still an early, untested category compared with the factory robots that dominate most humanoid news. Until a price, shipping date and independent reviews are available, it is hard to judge how Mobo will perform in real homes.
disclaimer: All specifications, sales and interest figures are AiMOGA's own claims from a press release and have not been independently verified.

title: Chinese humanoid makers seek factory and cafe trials in South Korea
summary: UBTech, Anyverse Dynamics and other Chinese firms are pursuing trials in South Korea as Seoul proposes 3.1 trillion won for physical AI, Korea Times reports.
body: Short answer: Chinese humanoid robot makers including UBTech, Anyverse Dynamics, AgiBot and Unitree are trying to win work in South Korea through factory trials and commercial projects as Seoul raises spending on physical AI, The Korea Times reported on 23 October 2026, in an article also published by the South China Morning Post.

According to the report, UBTech announced in July that it would trial humanoids on a Korean automotive parts line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker AJIN Industrial, and a UBTech executive said several models are undergoing on-site tests in the country, without giving details. The same executive said Seoul's Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue, bought UBTech's U1 model for around 170,000 yuan (about $25,000). Beijing start-up Anyverse Dynamics told the paper it plans trials in Korean cafes and other service settings in the fourth quarter before moving into manufacturing, and is working on product certification.

Chinese customs data cited in the report show South Korea was China's third-largest export market by value for "intelligent bionic robots" in the first nine months of 2026, at $19.99 million, behind the United States and Japan; the category, introduced this year, covers humanoid robots and robot dogs. The report says Korea's KC certification rules led UBTech to adapt its communication modules and radio settings for the local market.

On policy, the report says the government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (about $2.34 billion) for physical AI in 2027, more than triple this year's figure, and that the industry ministry's M.AX programme targets 500 AI factories by 2030. Korean companies are also active: the paper cites LG Electronics' robot data factory in Seoul, Samsung Electronics' new Robotics eXperience division and Hyundai Motor Group's training of Boston Dynamics' Atlas humanoids in Georgia ahead of a planned 2028 manufacturing deployment. A Counterpoint Research analyst told the paper the lack of locally built humanoids at scale has created an opening for Chinese suppliers, but that they need local customers willing to run proof-of-concept trials. We previously covered Korea's safety-rule exemption for a Robros factory pilot and China's humanoid output and standards push.
analysis: Opinion: South Korea pairs dense manufacturing with an aggressive policy push but few local humanoid suppliers at scale, which makes it a logical test market for Chinese makers. The report points to certification and finding local trial partners as the practical hurdles.
disclaimer: Figures are as reported by The Korea Times and the South China Morning Post, citing company executives, Chinese customs data and government plans; budget figures are proposals. This is not investment advice.

title: Why UCLA's PhoneBot, a small humanoid run by a smartphone, is getting attention
summary: UCLA's open-source PhoneBot uses an Android phone for sensing and computing in a 48 cm biped that its researchers say costs about $400 without the phone.
why: What happened: UCLA's RoMeLa lab described PhoneBot in an October 2026 arXiv preprint, New Atlas covered it on 12 October, and it appeared among X's trending robotics stories on 23 October.

Why it is being discussed: the low estimated parts cost of about $400 excluding the phone, and fully open hardware and software, compared with small research humanoids the paper lists at roughly $3,500 to $13,800 (arXiv, New Atlas).
What to watch: whether others build and extend the open design, and the limits the authors list, including no arms and walking trained only on flat ground.
body: Short answer: PhoneBot is a small open-source humanoid from UCLA's Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory (RoMeLa) that uses an ordinary Android smartphone as its camera, balance sensor, screen and main computer. The researchers estimate its parts cost at about $400 excluding the phone, according to their arXiv preprint and New Atlas, and the project was among X's trending robotics stories on 23 October 2026.

According to the paper, the robot is 48.3 cm tall, weighs 1.8 kg including the phone, and uses 13 low-cost servo motors: six in each leg plus one that turns the torso. The phone is not wired to the body; it sends joint commands over Wi-Fi to a small onboard computer that drives the motors, which the authors say makes it easier to swap in different phones.

The walking controller was trained in simulation with reinforcement learning, and the team reports demonstrations of walking, following a person using the phone's camera, and standing up from a face-down position. The researchers say they tested the app on four Android phones, including a 2017 Honor 9 and three prepaid models costing about $50 to $80, and that camera-based mapping did not run on the Honor 9. Speech recognition and the language model currently run on a nearby laptop rather than on the robot, the paper says.

The authors also list limitations: PhoneBot has no arms, its walking was trained only for flat ground, and its small motors limit what it can carry. The design files and code are open source and aimed at education and research, according to the project. For another example of low-cost humanoid research, see our report on Berkeley's SuperMimic controller trained on one GPU.
disclaimer: Cost and performance figures are the researchers' own, from a preprint and the project materials; they have not been independently verified. Cost comparisons with other platforms are approximate and not like-for-like.

title: Unitree says it is building "Rehearsal", a self-improving loop for robot software
summary: Unitree's Wang Xingxing said on 22 Oct 2026 the firm is developing "Rehearsal", a loop for robots to write code, test it in simulation and improve (SCMP).
body: Short answer: Unitree founder Wang Xingxing said on 22 October 2026 that the company is developing "Unitree Rehearsal", a "self-evolving" feedback loop designed to let humanoid robots write code, run simulations and improve their real-world performance with less manual programming, the South China Morning Post reported.

SCMP says Wang unveiled the project at a physical AI conference hosted by Unitree in Hangzhou and called it the company's most important initiative of the year. In the system under development, AI would search research papers, write code and test it in simulation before running trials on physical robots.
Humans could still assess performance and give feedback, according to SCMP, but Wang said the ultimate goal is an automated cycle that could greatly speed up the development of robotics algorithms.

PANews, summarising his keynote, reports that Wang said leading AI-model companies have in a sense already achieved self-evolution of models internally, and that the core challenge for embodied AI to have its "ChatGPT moment" is aligning AI model inputs and outputs with real robots. Neither report gives technical details, test results or a release date.
disclaimer: Rehearsal is described as under development, based on a keynote as reported by two outlets. No results have been published in the sources, so its capabilities are unproven.

title: Why Unitree's H2-X "Guardian" video is getting attention
summary: Unitree's H2-X teaser shows martial arts and staged rescue scenes; outlets note it released few specifications and it is unclear how autonomous the demos were.
body: Short answer: Unitree's H2-X "Kung Fu Legend Guardian" teaser video, released on 21 October 2026, has been widely covered because it shows a humanoid performing martial-arts moves and staged security and rescue scenes. Unitree has released few specifications, and outlets note it is unclear how autonomous the demos were.

Interesting Engineering, CNBC-TV18 and TechRadar describe the clip: kicks and punches that dent scrapyard cars, a jump from a platform marked four metres high, and staged scenes in which the robot steps between a woman and a person carrying a weapon, pushes a person away from an approaching car and lifts the front of a vehicle above a dummy.

On X, Unitree described the robot as offering "powerful performance to serve and guard you" with a maximum endurance of approximately eight hours, CNBC-TV18 reports; the on-screen safety text calls the figure standing time and advises staying two to three metres away. Interesting Engineering says the H2-X is based on Unitree's H2, which the company describes as about 1.8 metres tall and 70 kg. No price or release date has been announced, TechRadar and Interesting Engineering report.

Interesting Engineering and CNBC-TV18, the latter citing SCMP, say Unitree has not said whether the actions were autonomous, remotely controlled or pre-programmed. TechRadar calls the video more tech demo than consumer product and says it doubts such a robot could clear consumer certification as a personal bodyguard; that is the outlet's view, not Unitree's.
why: What happened: Unitree published a roughly one-minute promo for the H2-X on 21 October showing martial-arts moves and staged security and rescue scenes (TechRadar, Interesting Engineering).
Why it is being discussed: coverage focuses on how real the capabilities are, noting that autonomy, price and availability were not stated (Interesting Engineering, CNBC-TV18).
What to watch: whether Unitree publishes specifications, availability and how the demos were controlled.
disclaimer: Descriptions of the video and robot come from the company's own promotional material as reported by the outlets cited. We have not tested the robot, and its real-world performance is unverified.

title: Why Figure's nine-day Figure 03 treadmill test is getting attention
summary: Figure CEO Brett Adcock said a Figure 03 robot walked 348 miles over nine days on a treadmill; outlets note power and interruption details are unclear.
body: Short answer: Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock said on X on 19 October 2026 that a Figure 03 humanoid had walked on a treadmill for nine straight days, covering 348 miles and about 1.2 million steps in a test he said began as a side project to stress the robot for failures. The figures come from the company's CEO and have not been independently verified.

Interesting Engineering reports that a time-lapse shows the robot walking on a treadmill inside a testing facility with a power cable attached. Adcock's post ended with "Let's see how long it can go", which suggests the run was still going when he posted.

Both Interesting Engineering and TechRepublic note that details are unclear: whether one robot completed the whole run, how power and charging were handled, and whether there were interruptions or maintenance. TechRepublic says the result should not be read as nine days on a single battery charge.

For context, Interesting Engineering and TechRepublic recall Figure's May 2026 livestream of package sorting, which ran for about 200 hours and processed 249,560 packages, with several robots rotating through the task. The treadmill test instead emphasises accumulated walking distance and steps.
why: What happened: Brett Adcock said on 19 October that Figure 03 had walked 348 miles and about 1.2 million steps on a treadmill over nine days (Interesting Engineering, TechRepublic).
Why it is being discussed: Interesting Engineering describes it as a longer stress test meant to expose weaknesses that shorter demos might miss, while both outlets stress what remains unclear.
What to watch: independently verified endurance data, maintenance and uptime figures, and whether the test result is confirmed as a single robot's continuous run.
disclaimer: The test figures were reported by the company's CEO and relayed by news outlets; they have not been independently verified.

title: Tesla targets end of 2027 for external Optimus deliveries, Musk says
summary: Elon Musk said on Tesla's Q3 2026 earnings call that Tesla expects to start delivering Optimus robots to outside customers around the end of 2027, according to Electrek.
body: Short answer: Elon Musk said on Tesla's Q3 2026 earnings call that Tesla expects to begin delivering Optimus robots to outside customers around the end of 2027, once open issues with the AI, the hardware design and reliability are resolved, according to Electrek's report of the call.

Musk said Tesla has started early Optimus production at its Fremont factory in California, in an area that previously built Model S and Model X cars. He said most of the equipment for a line sized for one million robots a year is in place, but that reaching that pace could take a year or more because the design is still changing.

Asked what was still changing, a Tesla Optimus engineer pointed to the robot's hand and to custom gears with outstanding reliability concerns, Electrek reported. On AI, Musk said Tesla plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots to practise tasks in a programme it calls the "Optimus Academy", and to fit its AI5 chip to Optimus around April 2027.

Tesla expects its first outside customers to use Optimus for industrial work that is dangerous, repetitive or runs around the clock, Electrek reported. Electrek also notes that Tesla's earlier public targets for Optimus production and external sales were set for earlier years than this one.

title: Danish grocer Føtex pilots Unitree humanoids for overnight restocking
summary: Føtex, part of Salling Group, has started a multi-year pilot with HIVE Robots to train humanoid robots to restock shelves after closing time, ESM Magazine reports.
body: Short answer: Føtex, the Danish supermarket chain that is part of Salling Group, has started a multi-year pilot with Danish start-up HIVE Robots to train humanoid robots to restock shelves after closing time, ESM Magazine reports. The first trials are at a Føtex store in Lyngby, north of Copenhagen, ESM says, citing Euronews.

According to ESM, the robot hardware comes from the Chinese developer Unitree, while HIVE Robots writes the control software and handles the machine learning. Trials run outside opening hours so the robots can be tested and data collected without shoppers in the store.

To gather training data, human operators wearing VR headsets and using handheld controllers guide the robots through tasks such as lifting bags of pasta onto shelves, ESM reports. The current prototypes work more slowly than human staff, and developers expect AI progress to speed them up, it adds.

Simon Kudsk, Føtex's operations director, is quoted as saying that stores are designed around customers moving through them, which makes conventional industrial robots unsuitable, and that a human-shaped robot can move around the store naturally. ESM adds that Salling Group says the aim is to support staff rather than replace them, that HIVE Robots is targeting commercial deployment by early 2027 under an hourly service fee, and that Kudsk estimates a full rollout across the chain could take up to five years.

title: Berkeley's SuperMimic trains a humanoid motion controller in three hours on one GPU, authors report
summary: UC Berkeley researchers report that SuperMimic matched a baseline humanoid motion tracker that trained for seven days on 128 GPUs, using three hours on one GPU.
body: Short answer: UC Berkeley researchers report that a method called SuperMimic trained a humanoid whole-body motion controller in about three hours on a single GPU, surpassing the return of a baseline tracker that, per the authors, trained for seven days on 128 GPUs. The claims come from the paper's abstract and the project page; the authors list it as a CoRL 2026 paper.

The method learns to imitate a large library of human motions, 129,514 in the benchmark. Instead of training only inside a physics simulator, it fits one learned world model to logged simulator data and trains the control policy together with it, using gradients from short imagined rollouts, the authors explain.

The authors report using more than 1,000 times fewer GPU-hours than the baseline and failing on 25 of the 129,514 benchmark motions, against 179 for the baseline's released checkpoint. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs they report zero failures. They also say one policy runs on a physical Unitree G1 robot, including acrobatic motions.

The authors note several caveats themselves: the runs used different hardware (one NVIDIA H100 versus 128 L40 GPUs) and different amounts of motion data, and the benchmark motions are training motions, so the failure counts measure coverage rather than generalisation to new motions.
analysis: Analysis: If the results hold up under independent replication, much lower training cost could let smaller labs experiment with whole-body humanoid control. That is our reading, not a claim made in the sources.
disclaimer: This article summarises a research paper and project page by its authors. The results have not been independently replicated by us. It is not advice of any kind.

The companies say it is meant for humanoid research and development, scheduled to be available in early 2027, with planned integration of NVIDIA's Halos safety system. NVIDIA also claims the bundle cuts setup time "from weeks to days".

On the software side, NVIDIA says Isaac Lab 3.0 is now generally available and describes a new open-source Isaac OS runtime and a library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready robotics and factory assets.

title: Schaeffler opens Taicang factory where humanoids help build parts for humanoids
summary: Schaeffler says its new Taicang, China factory uses six humanoids to assemble joint modules, including actuators, for other humanoid robots.
body: Short answer: Schaeffler, the German motion-technology company, has opened a roughly 7,500 square metre "lighthouse" factory in Taicang, China, where six humanoid robots help assemble joint modules, including actuators, for other humanoid robots, the company said in a press release dated 20 October 2026.

According to Schaeffler, the six humanoids work across five stations on an assembly line the company developed. They stage and sort parts, join them, then inspect, label and package the finished modules. A digital twin mirrors the line in real time and logs measures such as assembly accuracy, step duration and energy use, so changes can be tested virtually before they reach the real line.

The site also holds a training and data-collection centre. Schaeffler says it trains humanoids there for tasks such as visual inspection, packaging, material handling, moving containers and line-side restocking, using set-ups modelled on conditions in its roughly 100 manufacturing plants. The company says the factory marks the start of mass production of these components for Schaeffler.

Schaeffler also says it added two customers from the Greater China region in the third quarter of 2026, lifting its global humanoid-robotics order intake to about 400 million euros. Gasgoo adds that Schaeffler Embodied Intelligence (Taicang) Co., Ltd. was set up in early 2026 to develop the site, and describes it as a platform for working with Chinese robotics companies.
disclaimer: This article summarises a company press release and one trade report. The order figure and production claims are Schaeffler's own and have not been independently verified. Schaeffler is a listed company; this is not investment advice.

title: Eka Robotics announces $150M Series A for force-sensing robot manipulation
summary: Eka Robotics said on 20 October 2026 it raised a $150 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and F-Prime; SiliconANGLE reports a $1.45 billion valuation.
body: Short answer: Eka Robotics, a robotics start-up, announced on 20 October 2026 a $150 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and F-Prime, a Fidelity Investments affiliate, according to SiliconANGLE and the company's announcement. SiliconANGLE reports a valuation of $1.45 billion.

Eka says it is building a "vision-force-action" model that combines camera images with force feedback from a custom gripper. It says the model is trained mostly in simulation using reinforcement learning, not by imitating human demonstrations, and that it is starting with dexterous manipulation, with examples such as packing fruit and assembling server racks.

The company reports its robots pick a wide range of objects not seen in training at about 1,500 operations per hour, against a human baseline of about 600 that Eka uses. SiliconANGLE adds that Eka told TechCrunch the robots handle objects up to one kilogram, succeed on more than 95% of picks, and are in pilots with industrial customers it has not named. These are company figures and have not been independently verified.

SiliconANGLE, citing TechCrunch, quotes Kris Hauser of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as saying a demo had a "wow factor" while questioning whether the system could run on an assembly line for a year without failure. He said it is still an open question whether it generalises beyond pick-and-place.

Eka says the new money will help extend the model to more tasks and speed up customer deployments. According to SiliconANGLE, the company was started last year by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and Tuomas Haarnoja, who joined from Google DeepMind, and investors have now put in about $161 million in total.
analysis: Analysis: Dexterous hands are widely seen as one of the hard problems for humanoid robots, so progress in force-sensing manipulation is relevant to the whole field. Eka's results so far are company-reported pick-and-place numbers, and independent, long-running trials would be needed to judge them.

title: China expects over 100,000 humanoid robots built in 2026 as first national standards approach
summary: A Chinese ministry official said China expects over 100,000 humanoids built in 2026, per China's SCIO; first national standards apply from April 2027.
body: Short answer: A senior Chinese industry ministry official said on 19 October 2026 that China expects to produce more than 100,000 humanoid robots this year, China's State Council Information Office (SCIO) reported. Separately, China's first six national standards for humanoid robots, announced in mid-October, take effect on 1 April 2027.

According to SCIO, Wei Wei, director general of the Department of Science and Technology at the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, told a Beijing press conference that China had developed more than 400 humanoid models by the end of June, with production above 40,000 units. He said products are being tested and deployed in more than 300 priority scenarios, including warehousing, logistics, catering, retail and household services.

The ministry plans to encourage retailers and other businesses to open their facilities to robot testing, to publish a 2026 edition of its guidelines for building a humanoid-robot standards system, and to set up a high-level open-source community, SCIO reported. Wei also said it will strengthen monitoring and testing of product quality, cybersecurity and data security while advancing ethical governance.

On the standards, CCTV reported on 16 October, citing the State Administration for Market Regulation, that six national standards were approved: five technical-requirements standards covering a humanoid's body, system architecture, environment perception and decision-making, plus one standard for simulation test platforms. MEKAWIRE, reading the national standards database, says they are recommended rather than mandatory, were issued on 28 September, and that Unitree, UBTech and Xiaomi's robot unit are listed among the drafters of all six.
disclaimer: Production figures and plans are official statements and forecasts, not guarantees. The standards are described from news reports and a database listing, not from the standard texts themselves. This article is not legal or compliance advice.

title: South Korea grants safety-rule exemption for 20 Robros humanoids in factory pilot
summary: A Korean regulatory-sandbox committee granted Robros an exemption so 20 of its humanoid robots can work near people at four companies' sites, Seoul Economic Daily reports.
body: Short answer: A South Korean regulatory-sandbox committee has granted the robot maker Robros an exemption from safety rules written for stationary industrial robots, so that 20 of its bipedal humanoid robots can work in spaces shared with or next to people at four companies' sites, Seoul Economic Daily reported on 14 October 2026.

The newspaper lists the sites as Nepes (semiconductors), Sungwoo Hitech (auto parts), HD Hyundai Samho (shipbuilding) and Delivery Lab (logistics). Tasks it names include removing contaminants from components, placing auto body parts, stacking scaffolding pieces and moving refrigerated packaging.

Before the exemption, the paper says, existing rules treated industrial robots as stationary equipment and required fences or other barriers between robots and human work areas. The exemption is conditional on risk assessments and safety measures, and data from the pilot is to inform future safety standards, according to the report.
Trade and Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan was quoted as saying that "AI technology is advancing so fast that regulation struggles to keep up".

title: Agility moves Digit 5 onto NVIDIA IGX Thor and expands in Pittsburgh
summary: Agility Robotics says Digit 5 will run on NVIDIA IGX Thor compute, and that it is opening a 50,000 sq ft Pittsburgh hub and holds over $300M in multi-year Digit 5 orders.
body: Short answer: Agility Robotics said on 22 October 2026 that the general-availability version of its Digit 5 humanoid will standardise its onboard computing on NVIDIA IGX Thor modules, making NVIDIA the exclusive onboard compute supplier. A day earlier, on 21 October, the company announced a new 50,000-square-foot facility in Pittsburgh and said it has secured more than $300 million in multi-year Digit 5 orders, subject to contractual milestones, according to its press releases.

According to Agility, the change unifies Digit 5's onboard computing on NVIDIA IGX Thor modules and builds on its earlier decision to incorporate elements of NVIDIA's Halos safety platform into its own safety system, including the way Digit detects people around it. The company says it will also take part in NVIDIA's Halos AI Systems Inspection Lab, which will evaluate Digit's safety-related software, AI components and cybersecurity protections ahead of final third-party certification. Agility says early access to Digit 5 should begin in the first half of 2027, with availability widening over the following six to nine months for manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators.

The Pittsburgh site, Agility says, will add about 35,000 square feet to its existing footprint in the city and serve as its centre of excellence for software and AI, and increase its capacity to deploy, monitor and service Digit robots for customers. The company says Digit already operates with GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, and that it has added four customers in automotive, consumer goods and agriculture, including a pilot with farm-machinery maker AGCO.

The $300 million figure needs context: Agility says the orders are subject to the satisfaction of certain contractual milestones, and it did not name the customers behind them. The Next Web reported that the announcements come as Agility prepares to list on Nasdaq through a merger with a blank-check company, Churchill Capital Corp XI, which the companies expect to close in the fourth quarter.
analysis: Opinion: Standardising on one compute platform and pairing it with an outside safety inspection is the kind of unglamorous step that matters more for factory deployment than a new demo video. The order figure is large, but it depends on milestones and robot deployments that are still more than a year away, so the 2027 early-access programme is the thing to watch.
disclaimer: Order values, deployment plans and timelines are Agility Robotics' own statements and have not been independently verified; the company describes the order figure as potential multi-year value, not current revenue.
