title: Figure says Figure 04 is in design lock and teases Helix 3.0 in a public all-hands
summary: In a published all-hands recording, Figure CEO Brett Adcock said Figure 04 has reached design lock, its Index app has 37.5 million human videos, and previewed Helix 3.0.
body: Short answer: Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock published a recording of an internal all-hands meeting on 22 October 2026 in which he said the company's fourth-generation humanoid, Figure 04, has reached design lock, gave new figures for its human-video data programme, and teased its next AI model, Helix 3.0, according to reports by Humanoids Daily and TechRadar.

According to Humanoids Daily, Adcock said Figure 04's actuators were running in the test lab, ten full battery packs had been brought up the previous week, and the hand was on its fourth iteration, with months of work on millimetre-level fingertip tracking. He said Figure built its 1,000th Figure 03 over the summer, the outlet reported. TechRadar, writing on 24 October, said the Figure 03 production run is now in four figures.

On data, Adcock said Figure's Index app had received 37.5 million video uploads across 112 countries, with 1.26 million downloads and 210,000 people uploading at least one video in the previous week, and an estimated $8.1 million spent on data that week, according to Humanoids Daily. The outlet notes these are company-reported numbers and that uploads are not the same as cleaned training footage. Adcock also reported more than $2 billion in cash and referred to Figure's compute agreement with Nscale, and said Figure robots are operating in three US states.

The presentation closed with a Helix 3.0 teaser. Adcock described an internal result as "baby AGI" but did not share evaluation details or a release date, Humanoids Daily reported. Figure has not yet shown Figure 04 publicly. Earlier this month Figure also drew attention for a long-running Figure 03 treadmill test.
analysis: Opinion: Figure's bet is that huge volumes of human video plus large compute will produce general-purpose robot skills. The numbers are striking, but they describe inputs, not outcomes; until Figure publishes how Helix 3.0 performs on real tasks, the 'baby AGI' label is a claim rather than a result.

title: Alibaba's Amap team releases λ0, a humanoid model trained largely on human video
summary: Researchers at Alibaba's Amap and Token Hub released λ0, a whole-body humanoid model trained on a 500-hour human video dataset; they report 62.5% success on four real-world tasks with a Unitree G1.
body: Short answer: A team from Alibaba Group's Amap mapping business and its Token Hub unit has released λ0 (lambda zero), a model for controlling a humanoid robot's whole body that learns much of what it knows from first-person video of people. In a preprint on arXiv, the team reports that λ0 succeeded in 62.5% of real-world trials across four tasks on a Unitree G1 robot, compared with 40% for π0.5, the strongest rival it tested. The results have not been peer reviewed or reproduced by outside groups.

According to the paper, the key ingredient is HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of people doing everyday tasks while wearing a GoPro camera at a height matching the robot's own camera, with wearable trackers recording their body movement and hand motion reconstructed from the video. The team trains λ0 in stages, using HumanVerse in a middle stage before final tuning on robot demonstrations. The authors estimate human capture is roughly 3.4 times faster than collecting robot data, TSN reported.

The real-world tests covered four tasks with ten trials each, run by the authors on a Unitree G1 fitted with dexterous hands. The authors report that skipping the HumanVerse stage cut real-world success to 22.5%, which they present as the main evidence that the human data matters. They also report 90% success on the SIMPLE simulation benchmark, but note that this figure picks the best configuration per task and should not be read as a fixed-configuration comparison.

The code is available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 licence, and TSN reported on 24 October that a mid-training checkpoint has been published on Hugging Face, while the HumanVerse dataset and the full final training and deployment workflows have not yet been released. The work comes as other companies, including Figure with its Index video programme, also bet on human video to train robots.
analysis: Opinion: The most persuasive number here is the team comparing its own model with and without human data, not the league table against rivals, which rests on ten trials per task run by the authors themselves. Independent groups will only be able to test the central claim once the dataset is released.

XPENG attributes the behaviour to its VLA 2.0 system, which it says reassesses what the robot sees every 0.2 seconds.

When the tester moves a high five out of reach of the arm IRON is using, the robot answers with its other hand. XPENG says the upgraded model has stronger temporal understanding and behaviour prediction and runs on the robot itself, Humanoid Guide reported.

Both outlets note the limits of what was shown. According to Humanoids Daily, the footage is labelled as an R&D test version, and XPENG did not disclose success rates, how many attempts were filmed, or end-to-end response times; the 0.2-second figure describes how often the model updates, not how long a full response takes. XPENG CEO He Xiaopeng described the demo as a step toward everyday use, the outlet reported.

Humanoids Daily reports that XPENG is targeting mass production and first deliveries of IRON in the fourth quarter of 2026. Other recent humanoid demos have also drawn close scrutiny, such as Unitree's H2-X guardian video.
analysis: Opinion: Reacting to a gesture that changes halfway through is a small but genuinely useful skill for robots meant to work around people. Without success rates or unedited trials, though, the clip shows what the system can do on a good take, not how reliably it does it.

title: ETH Zürich's ACP policy lets a Unitree G1 climb ladders, vault and get back up after falls
seo_title: ETH Zürich ACP: humanoid climbs, vaults and recovers
summary: Researchers at ETH Zürich's Robotic Systems Lab report a single learned policy, Attention-based Contact Planning, that plans where a humanoid's hands, knees, feet and pelvis should touch the terrain, letting a Unitree G1 climb, vault and recover from falls.
body: Short answer: A team led by ETH Zürich's Robotic Systems Lab has shown a Unitree G1 humanoid climbing ladders, vaulting obstacles and getting back up after falls using one learned control policy, according to Humanoids Daily. The method, called Attention-based Contact Planning (ACP), decides where parts of the robot's body should touch the environment and lets a second network work out the movement in between.

According to the outlet, the planner uses a height map built from a head-mounted LiDAR, the robot's own sensed state and a target position to predict contact points up to 1.5 seconds ahead for nine body parts: the hands, elbows, knees, feet and pelvis. A second network turns those targets into commands for 23 joints, and both run on the robot at 50 Hz without replaying a pre-recorded motion. The team trained the system with 13.2 minutes of human motion data plus reinforcement learning, Humanoids Daily reported.

The researchers report 92.5% average success across eight simulated obstacle courses, compared with 58.8% for a motion-generation-and-tracking baseline. Humanoids Daily stresses that this is a simulation figure, measured with sensor noise and physics randomisation switched off, and not a real-world success rate. The project also publishes failure and recovery clips, including a fall caused by mapping errors.

The paper, titled Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts, was submitted to arXiv on 22 October and is listed as under review, according to the outlet, which says the project credits ETH Zürich, Apple, the ETH AI Center and NVIDIA. The authors list limits including overhead contacts, hanging and manipulation. It is one of several recent G1 research projects, alongside Amazon's whole-body dexterity work and Alibaba's λ0 model.
analysis: Opinion: Planning contacts rather than full poses is an appealing middle layer, because it gives a robot a reason to use its knees or pelvis the way people do on rough ground. Until real-world success rates are published, the clips show capability rather than reliability.

title: Amazon-led team teaches a humanoid to hold boxes against its torso and under its arm
seo_title: Amazon Whole-Body Dexterity: humanoid uses torso to carry
summary: A preprint from Amazon, UC San Diego and the University of Michigan describes Whole-Body Dexterity, a controller that lets a teleoperated Unitree G1 brace objects against its arms and torso, completing 45 of 50 real-world trials.
body: Short answer: Researchers from Amazon, the University of California, San Diego and the University of Michigan have published Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a method that lets a humanoid robot use its arms and torso, not just its hands, to hold and move objects. In real-world tests on a Unitree G1, the authors report that their controller completed 45 of 50 trials (90%), compared with 18% for direct motion retargeting and 4% for a general-purpose whole-body controller.

According to the arXiv preprint, the team first generated about 2.5 million simulated grasps that use the arms and torso, trained reinforcement-learning "experts" to move objects between those grasps, then distilled them into a single controller that needs only the robot's own joint readings and the object's rough dimensions. On the real robot, the tasks were moving a basketball or a 15 cm cardboard box to the shoulder or under one arm and back, plus a longer sequence of picking a box from a shelf, tucking it under an arm, walking it to a table and setting it down.

The robot was not acting on its own. The paper says every real-world trial was run by a single skilled human teleoperator wearing a motion-capture suit, with the WBD controller adjusting the arm commands to keep the object supported. In the shelf task, the controller finished all five stages in 7 of 10 trials and occasionally dropped the box, the authors report. The work is a preprint on arXiv.
Latest Robot News covered the paper on 25 October. The authors list the project site as wholebodydex.com. Other recent G1 research includes ETH Zürich's contact-planning policy.
analysis: Opinion: Carrying things against the body is how people handle bulky items, so this is a practical direction for warehouse-style work. The heavy reliance on a trained teleoperator means it is a better assistive controller today than an autonomous skill.

Vuntum adds that Yaskawa invested in Japanese AI company Noetra in July.

HuRoC adds that in earlier investor Q&A Yaskawa said it is not focused on two-legged walking and is considering an upper-body robot mounted on a mobile base, the layout used by Tokyo Robotics' Torobo, which the startup's site lists as in development at 1,615 mm tall with arms that can each carry up to 7 kg. body: Short answer: Japan's two largest carmakers are testing humanoid robots on real production tasks. Toyota and Honda are trialling the machines on work ranging from installing wire harnesses to carrying out final inspections, according to Automotive News, whose reporting was relayed on 26 October by Seeking Alpha and TokenPost. Both companies showed their latest machines at the 2026 Japan Mobility Show in Tokyo.

Honda's exhibit centred on its Avatar Robot, which Automotive News describes as using artificial intelligence to carry out delicate, complicated tasks with robotic human-like hands. Toyota is testing how humanoids handle assembly work; the Robot Daily reports the company has said it aims to roll out large numbers of factory robots from 2028, including its wheeled ELEY humanoid, which learns tasks from line workers.

Wire harnesses are a long-standing automation problem because the cables are flexible and must be routed by hand through the car body. Neither company has published trial volumes, success rates or a deployment date for humanoids on these tasks in the reports we cite.
The trials join a wider push by carmakers: see our coverage of FAW-Volkswagen's logistics tests with UBTECH and of Yaskawa's humanoid plans. More is on our pilots and deployments page.

title: Google opens Gemini Robotics ER 2, a high-level 'robot brain' model, to cloud customers in public preview
seo_title: Gemini Robotics ER 2 enters public preview on Google Cloud
summary: Google says its Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 model, which plans and checks tasks for robots from arms to humanoids, is now in public preview on its Gemini platform for enterprise developers.
body: Short answer: Google has made Gemini Robotics Embodied Reasoning 2 (ER 2) available in public preview on its Gemini platform, according to a Google Cloud blog post published on 27 October 2026 by Carolina Parada, head of Google DeepMind's robotics team, and Adrian Jones. Google describes ER 2 as a robot's high-level reasoning model that plans multi-step tasks and directs lower-level control systems, and says it works across robot types from stationary arms to full humanoids.

In Google's description, ER 2 does not move motors directly. Developers declare low-level interfaces, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models, navigation APIs or custom functions, as tools that the model can call, and stream video, audio or text into it. Google says the model can then plan long tasks involving hundreds of decisions, check from video whether a step actually succeeded, retry failed steps without restarting a whole workflow, and coordinate teams of different robots that share an understanding of the workspace.

The post gives some company-reported figures: Google says ER 2 pinpoints the video frame at which a key event happens, such as when to stop pouring a liquid, with 91.3% accuracy and a mean error of 0.96 seconds, and that it can read values from more than ten kinds of instruments, including dials, sight glasses, digital displays and thermometers. Google also points to tooling for testing behaviours in simulators such as MuJoCo-Warp and NVIDIA Isaac Sim, labelling demonstration videos, and training custom VLA models on its cloud.

The announcement includes supportive comments from Boston Dynamics about its Spot quadruped inspection product, from data-collection start-up DeepReach, from Arm, and from A*STAR's materials research institute, which said it wants to use the model to help lab robots work with existing equipment. Google did not publish pricing in the post itself; it links to separate documentation and a DeepMind technical report. For other recent work on humanoid foundation models, see our report on Alibaba Amap's Lambda-0 and our research hub.
analysis: Opinion: Splitting a robot's software into a general 'planner' model and separate low-level skill models is becoming a common pattern, and putting the planner behind a cloud API lowers the barrier for humanoid makers that do not train their own large models. The figures are Google's own benchmarks, so independent tests on real humanoid deployments will matter more than the launch numbers.

title: Samsung is developing five-finger, tendon-style robot hands for its humanoid, Korean paper reports

summary: The Hankyoreh reports that Samsung Electronics' new robotics division is building a humanoid with cable-driven, five-fingered hands, as Korean groups prepare humanoid showings ahead of CES 2027.
body: Short answer: Samsung Electronics is developing a humanoid robot with five fingers on each hand, using cables that pull the fingers in a way similar to human tendons, the Korean newspaper The Hankyoreh reported on 27 October 2026, citing industry officials. The work sits in Samsung's Robotics eXperience (RX) division, which the paper says was set up in July by combining the company's robot research and commercialisation teams and reports directly to the CEO.

According to the report, Samsung's chairman was expected to visit the RX division at the company's research campus in Seocho, Seoul, to see a demonstration of the robot's hands picking up and handling objects. The paper also said Samsung has been focusing on hand manipulation and has recruited people who previously led robotics strategy at Boston Dynamics, the Hyundai Motor Group company. Samsung has not published technical details of the hands.

The Hankyoreh contrasts different design choices among Korean groups. Boston Dynamics' new Atlas uses four fingers per hand, which the paper says simplifies the drive mechanism and reduces load on the actuators, and Hyundai plans to deploy Atlas at its car plant in Georgia, US, from 2028. LG Electronics' CLOiD home robot and Tesla's Optimus have five-fingered hands, and LG Group has said it will work with NVIDIA on a bipedal humanoid due to be unveiled in the first quarter of 2027, the report said.

Experts quoted by the paper noted that finger count alone does not decide dexterity: degrees of freedom, joint range and touch sensors matter too. KAIST professor Park Hae-won told the paper that five-finger hands make it easier to reuse training data recorded from human hand motion. The paper expects CES 2027 in January to show how commercially ready the Korean groups' humanoids are. For more on Korea's humanoid market, see our report on Chinese humanoid makers seeking trials in South Korea.
analysis: Opinion: Hands are where many humanoid demos still look weakest, so a large electronics maker putting its effort there is notable. Tendon-driven hands can be compact and human-like but are harder to keep calibrated over long use; durability data, not a first demo, will show whether the approach is practical in factories.

title: Imperial spinout Machenta raises $40 million seed round for robots that learn a task from one demonstration
seo_title: Machenta raises $40M seed for one-demo robot learning
summary: London-based Machenta, spun out of Imperial College London, says its simulation-trained model lets robots, including humanoids, learn new tasks after seeing them done once.
body: Short answer: Machenta, a robotics AI start-up spun out of Imperial College London, has raised a $40 million seed round co-led by Creandum and Union Square Ventures, Imperial announced on 27 October 2026. Imperial describes it as the largest seed round raised by a UK robotics start-up. Machenta is building a robot foundation model that it says can learn a new physical task from a single demonstration.

The company was founded by Edward Johns, Professor of Robot Learning at Imperial, who is chief executive, and his PhD student Vitalis Vosylius, together with colleagues from Imperial's Robot Learning Lab, where the underlying research began about six years ago. According to Imperial, the team has shown a single model learning varied tasks such as packing and tidying across different robots, including humanoid robots. Tech.eu reported that Johns likens the approach to "physical vibe coding".

A key difference from many current robot models, according to the company, is that Machenta's model is pre-trained entirely on simulated data rather than large collections of real-world human demonstrations. Imperial says this could help developers avoid the practical and privacy limits of gathering large amounts of human data. Tech.eu reported that the team numbers around a dozen people.

Machenta plans to use the money to scale its model and grow its team at a new office and lab in King's Cross, London, Imperial said. The valuation was not disclosed in the announcements we reviewed. For other recent humanoid funding news, see our funding and policy hub and our report on Eka Robotics' Series A.
analysis: Opinion: Data collection is one of the biggest costs in robot learning, so a credible way to pre-train only in simulation would matter to every humanoid maker. One-demonstration learning has looked impressive in labs before; the test is how reliably it holds up on unfamiliar objects and robots outside curated demos.

body: Short answer: Robotics company Reward AI posted video on X on 27 October 2026 showing humanoid robots, controlled by its OM-1 model, taking parcels out of a vehicle for last-mile delivery and grasping objects while standing on stairs. The company says the clips are autonomous. By the morning of 28 October the main post had passed 320,000 views on X.

In follow-up posts, Reward AI said it had stress-tested the model on parcels placed in different positions and orientations, and that the robots adjust their approach, climb and descend stairs while holding the package. French site RoboActu, which covered the demo on 28 October, described how the robot adapts to a parcel's position before picking it up and moving off with the load.

According to the company, the model learns from people wearing a capture device, including a seven-degree-of-freedom glove called Omnibody Hand that records hand movement, contact and force, rather than from teleoperated robots, and the company says it does not use robot-collected data to train the general policy. Reward AI also says a new task can be learned from under 30 minutes of human demonstrations.

RoboActu noted that the videos are the company's own communication and that Reward AI did not publish success rates, numbers of attempts, comparisons with other models or customer-site results alongside them. For other recent work on humanoids carrying loads, see our report on Amazon researchers' whole-body carrying study and our research hub.

title: AGIBOT pitches 'Worken' as a measure of useful robot work and shows AHA3, GO-3 Preview and G2 Max
seo_title: AGIBOT Worken metric, AHA3, GO-3 and G2 Max explained
summary: At its Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai on 29 October, AGIBOT proposed a robot productivity metric called Worken and showed a third-generation humanoid architecture, new AI models, the G2 Max robot and an open-source operating system plan, according to the company.
body: Short answer: AGIBOT used its Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai on 29 October to argue that humanoid makers should be judged on the useful work their robots do, not on how many they ship, and it proposed a metric called Worken to measure that, according to the company's announcement. It also showed new hardware, AI models and an operating system plan.

According to AGIBOT, Worken (a blend of "work" and "token") stands for "Effective Intelligent Work Hours" and is calculated as the number of active robots multiplied by their autonomous working hours and an output-efficiency ratio. Co-founder, president and CTO Peng Zhihui introduced it, saying the real question for robots is "how much productive work are they actually delivering?", the company said.

On hardware, AGIBOT presented AHA3, the third generation of its AGIBOT Humanoid Architecture. The company lists Wi-Fi 6 and 5G connectivity, liquid cooling in the joints, IP67-rated joints, a family of OmniHand 3 hands (Lite, standard and Ultra) and an OmniPicker 3 gripper with tactile sensing. It also showed the G2 Max, which it says has 21 degrees of freedom, can handle up to 40 kg with both arms and works at heights from 0.1 m to 2.5 m.

On software, AGIBOT previewed GO-3, which it describes as a World Reasoning Action Model (WRAM), and WITA-Omni, a full-duplex interaction model designed to run on the robot. AGIBOT says GO-3 Preview placed first on the RoboDojo and RoboColiseum evaluations and scored highest on RoboTwin, and that WITA-Omni ranks first on Daily-Omni. Humanoids Daily notes that these rankings are reported by AGIBOT and were not independently checked.

AGIBOT also announced Link-U OS 1.0, a robot operating system that it says selected partners are trialling now and that will be fully open source by the end of 2026, with the project donated to the OpenAtom Foundation. The company says its developer ecosystem spans 255 universities, 511 enterprises and more than 80,000 developers.

The company pointed to work in tablet production for Longcheer, semiconductor packaging, CNC machine tending, Guangzhou Metro and the Chimelong resort group as examples of deployments, according to the announcement. Humanoids Daily adds that AGIBOT built its 20,000th robot in September 2026. AGIBOT previously drew attention with a 110-robot synchronised dance record; more Chinese humanoid coverage is on our China hub.
analysis: Opinion: A shared way to count useful robot hours would help buyers compare vendors, but Worken is only as good as the data behind it. Until independent customers or auditors publish Worken figures, it is best read as AGIBOT's own yardstick rather than an industry standard.

title: Why Tau Robotics' humanoid home-cleaning subscription is trending
seo_title: Why Tau Robotics humanoid home cleaning is trending
summary: A 29 October post from Tau Robotics' founder announcing recurring bookings for its supervised humanoid cleaners in San Francisco passed 670,000 views on X within a day. Here is what the service is, according to the company, and what to watch.
body: Short answer: On 29 October, Tau Robotics founder and CEO Alexander Koch posted on X that customers can now book the company's humanoid cleaners on a recurring subscription, for up to three hours per visit. The post, with a video Koch described as a first, uncut take shown at four times speed, had passed 670,000 views by the morning of 30 October, according to X's public post metrics.

Tau's website describes the robots doing dusting, wiping surfaces, cleaning toilets, vacuuming and mopping, and says the company usually sends two robots per cleaning. According to the same FAQ, the robots are not fully autonomous: they are operated by humans and AI, and a human supervisor decides when a robot works on its own and when to steer it directly.

The booking page says access is invite-only with a waitlist, that every clean is supervised by a remote human operator, and that bathrooms and bedrooms are off-limits by default unless the customer opts in. A repeating clean is billed per visit and can be cancelled at any time, according to the page.

On price, the San Francisco Chronicle reported in July 2026 that Tau launched at $30 an hour. The company's terms of service, last updated on 24 October 2026, list a standard fee of $50 per humanoid per hour and say the price shown at booking is the price the customer pays, so the amount charged may vary with discounts or offers.

According to the Chronicle, Tau was founded in 2024, had raised $2.6 million in pre-seed funding and aims to move the human operator over time toward safety supervision only, and eventually to remove the need for one. Koch told the paper that home cleaning is "a useful starting point for humanoids". For other at-home humanoid efforts, see our coverage of Reward AI's delivery demo and AiMOGA's family companion robot.
why: What happened: Tau Robotics' CEO announced recurring subscriptions for its supervised humanoid cleaning service in San Francisco on 29 October, with a video that he described as an uncut first take.

Why it is being discussed: The post drew more than 4,500 likes, about 600 replies and more than 260 quote posts in its first day, according to X's public metrics, and X featured the service in a trending story. Humanoids doing chores in real homes, with a human operator in the loop, is a concrete and easy-to-picture use case.
What to watch: Whether Tau publishes how much of each clean is done autonomously, whether it opens booking beyond invites and San Francisco, and how its listed prices settle.
analysis: Opinion: Openly saying that a remote operator supervises every visit is the right call. It sets honest expectations, and the share of work done without a human taking over is the number that will show whether this becomes a scalable service.

title: US calls robot imports a national security risk but opts for trade talks, not new tariffs, for now
seo_title: Section 232 robotics proclamation: what it means for humanoids
summary: A 28 October White House proclamation names humanoid and quadruped robots among advanced robots that support the US military and orders trade negotiations on robotics and industrial machinery imports, with an update due within 180 days and no new tariffs for now.
body: Short answer: On 28 October 2026, President Donald J. Trump issued a proclamation agreeing with the Commerce Secretary's Section 232 finding that imports of robotics, industrial machinery and their parts threaten to impair US national security. It directs negotiations with trading partners rather than imposing new tariffs at this stage, according to the proclamation and an EY Tax News alert.

Humanoids are named directly. According to The Robot Report, the proclamation cites "advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles" as providing direct support to the US military.

According to EY's summary, the Commerce findings cover the role of these machines in defence production, their use across all 16 US critical infrastructure sectors, US reliance on imports with growing import values over the last decade, potential cybersecurity risk from equipment sourced from certain foreign entities, and domestic production that is not sufficient to meet national security needs.

Under the plan, the Commerce Secretary and the US Trade Representative will pursue agreements with trading partners and must update the President at least once within 180 days of 28 October. EY says the proclamation allows the President to consider other remedies depending on how talks go, including tariffs, duties, quotas, fees and a programme to encourage new US production investment. EY also notes that existing Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminium and copper are not changed, and that no specific product codes have been identified yet.

Industry reaction gathered by The Robot Report treated the move as a signal rather than an immediate cost. Ash Sharma of Interact Analysis told the publication it should not be read as "a new robotics tariff today" but as an indication of direction. The White House fact sheet sets out the administration's reasoning. For context on supply and policy elsewhere, see our pieces on China's humanoid output and standards and Chinese makers seeking trials in South Korea, and our funding and policy hub.
analysis: Opinion: For humanoid makers selling into the US, the 180-day window is the date to plan around. Many humanoids rely on imported actuators, gears and sensors, so any later measure on components could matter as much as one on finished robots.

summary: Audi, Agile Robots, Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA are running a proof of concept in Audi's Production Lab in which mobile humanoids pick car parts from containers and place them in assembly order, with the Ingolstadt plant as the target, according to the companies and trade press.
body: Short answer: Audi and Munich-based Agile Robots, supported by Dassault Systèmes and NVIDIA, are testing whether mobile humanoids can take on parts sequencing, the job of picking parts from containers and laying them out in the order final assembly needs them, according to a joint Audi media release. The proof of concept runs in the Audi Production Lab and is aimed at the Ingolstadt plant, as Automotive Logistics reported on 28 October.

The project was first announced at NVIDIA GTC Berlin on 21 October, according to Audi and Agile Robots, and has drawn fresh coverage this week. Audi says sequencing at its sites involves around one million picks a day, which makes it one of the more demanding automation tasks in its logistics.

According to the release, the partners use a virtual twin built with Dassault Systèmes' DELMIA on the 3DEXPERIENCE platform, together with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, to test feasibility, cycle timing, ergonomics and safety before robots work on the real line. The release adds that LEO, Dassault Systèmes' AI-powered virtual companion, is set to assist engineers in future.

Interesting Engineering reported on 29 October that the robots are Agile ONE humanoids and that no performance results or rollout timeline have been given. Agile Robots says it was founded in 2018, has more than 20,000 solutions deployed and employs over 3,500 people.

Agile Robots unveiled its Agile ONE SN reference humanoid at the same event, as covered in our report on NVIDIA's Isaac update. Other carmakers are running similar trials, including FAW-Volkswagen with UBTech and Toyota and Honda in Japan; more are on our deployments hub.
analysis: Opinion: Sequencing is a sensible target because it is repetitive, high-volume and already happens in a structured area. A proof of concept is still a long way from series use, though, and pick rates and error rates will decide whether it reaches Ingolstadt's line.

title: X-Era releases E0.5, an open robot model that predicts the 3D scene ahead, tested on a Zerith H1 humanoid
seo_title: X-Era E0.5 3D world-action model, open source
summary: X-Era AI's E0.5 builds a robot control model on a 3D foundation model and trains it to predict future scene geometry. The team has released code and a checkpoint, and reports real-robot gains on a dual-arm system and a Zerith H1 humanoid.
body: Short answer: X-Era AI has published E0.5, a world-action model that uses a 3D vision model as its backbone and learns to predict how the scene will look in 3D at the end of each chunk of robot motion, according to the team's technical report, submitted to arXiv on 26 October 2026. Code is on GitHub and a RoboTwin checkpoint is on Hugging Face; RoboSignal covered the release on 29 October.

Most world-action models start from a video generator or a vision-language model, the authors write. E0.5 instead starts from VGGT-Omega, a model built to reconstruct depth, 3D points and camera poses, and trains it end to end to predict the future depth, point maps and camera parameters alongside the robot's actions. According to the project page, the future-geometry output is used only as a training signal and is removed when the robot is deployed.

In the RoboTwin 2.0 simulation benchmark, the team reports 89.90% success in clean scenes and 50.09% in randomised scenes across 50 tasks, with a 2.32-billion-parameter policy and no robot-data pretraining. Predicting future geometry rather than only reconstructing the current scene added about 7.9 percentage points of average success in its tests, the report says.

The team then pretrained E0.5 on more than 160,000 trajectories from the AgiBotWorld-Beta dataset and tested it on an AgileX Piper dual-arm system and the Zerith H1 humanoid on three tabletop jobs: placing a mouse on a pad, packing a charger and its cable into a basket, and putting rubbish in a bin. According to the project page, mean real-world success on the H1 rose from 81.7% to 88.3% with that pretraining, and from 70.0% to 85.0% on the Piper. Each setting used 10 trials per task, the report says.

The GitHub page says the release includes training and inference code and RoboTwin evaluation tools, and the Hugging Face model card describes the posted checkpoint as an intermediate one rather than the final model. For related research, see our coverage of Alibaba Amap's λ0 model, Machenta's one-demonstration learning and our research hub.
analysis: Opinion: Putting geometry at the centre is an interesting bet against video-first robot models, and releasing code makes it testable. The real-robot trials are small (10 per task), so independent reproductions on more humanoids will matter more than the headline percentages.
disclaimer: Benchmark and real-robot results are as reported by the X-Era AI authors in a preprint that has not been peer reviewed.

title: Agility Robotics expects about $465 million from its Churchill XI deal and plans to trade on Nasdaq as AGLT

summary: Agility Robotics and Churchill Capital Corp XI expect about $465 million in gross capital, a 4 November close and AGLT trading on Nasdaq from 5 November.
body: Short answer: Agility Robotics, the maker of the Digit humanoid, and the blank-check company Churchill Capital Corp XI expect their merger to bring in gross capital of about $465 million before transaction expenses, according to a joint announcement on 30 October 2026. The companies expect the deal to close on 4 November, with the combined company's shares expected to start trading on Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT on 5 November.

According to the announcement, the total is made up of about $164 million left in Churchill XI's trust account after its redemption deadline passed, about $201 million in common stock PIPE commitments at $10.00 per share led by Foxconn, and $100 million in equity that Agility says it already received after the deal was first announced. Churchill XI shareholders are due to vote at an extraordinary general meeting on 2 November.

Agility says it has a pipeline of more than 30 prospective customers across manufacturing, automotive, aerospace, defense, logistics and consumer products. The announcement repeats news from 26 October that GXO plans to put Digit into two more facilities, that AGCO expects to start a pilot in 2027 and that three more manufacturing customers have joined paid programs. We covered those updates in our stories on GXO's expansion and the AGCO pilot.

The company also says it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5, the next-generation robot it showed on 15 September 2026, with early-access deliveries planned for the first half of 2027 and general availability by the end of 2027. Agility notes that this figure is a potential multi-year value that depends on milestones being met and is not current revenue. More on that robot is in our Digit 5 story.

Investors in Agility listed in the announcement include NVIDIA, Amazon, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Schaeffler, Foxconn, Abico, DCVC and Playground Global. Existing Agility shareholders are rolling their equity into the combined company and have agreed to a 180-day lock-up, according to the announcement, which also says the two companies' joint registration statement was declared effective by the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 13 October. More coverage is on our Agility Robotics hub and funding and policy hub.

The more useful test will be how much of the Digit 5 order book turns into delivered robots and recurring revenue once early-access units ship in 2027.

title: Why a report of December Tesla Optimus reservations is trending, and why it is disputed
seo_title: Why the Tesla Optimus reservations report is trending
summary: A report that Tesla would open Optimus reservations in December spread fast on 30 October, then Elon Musk replied "No" on X. Here is what each side said.
body: Short answer: On 30 October, The San Francisco Standard reported that Tesla planned to open reservations for its Optimus humanoid in early December. Hours later, Tesla CEO Elon Musk replied "No" to a post on X asking whether Optimus ordering was coming in December, which the Standard said appeared to deny the plan. Tesla has not published an ordering or reservation page, so the timing remains unclear.

According to the Standard, the claim came from Modar Alaoui, an investor at ALM Ventures who runs The Humanoids Summit, which takes place in San Mateo on 1 and 2 December. Alaoui told the paper that Tesla had told him reservations would open with his event or in the days after it, that most robots would go to companies with a small number for consumers, and that he expected the first shipments to include the Optimus V3. The Standard put the expected price at more than $20,000, said Tesla did not respond to requests for comment, said it was unclear how much money, if any, would be needed to reserve one, and said the robots would likely not ship for another year.

The Standard's reporter, Rachyl Jones, posted the news on X at 19:05 UTC on 30 October. Two minutes later, tech commentator Robert Scoble quoted it, asking whether ordering was coming in December and jokingly asking the @Bot account to watch for it and order him one. Musk answered that post at 22:08 UTC with a single word, "No".

TeslaNorth noted that Musk was replying to a post that mixed the question with a joke, so it is not fully clear which part he was answering. The Standard's report also recalled Musk's comments on Tesla's latest earnings call, where he said Optimus still had issues with its AI, electromechanical design and runtime that he expected to be solved around the end of next year, which is when he said to expect deliveries to companies outside Tesla. Our earlier story on Tesla's late 2027 delivery target has more background.
why: What happened: The San Francisco Standard reported, based on comments from a summit organiser, that Tesla would open Optimus reservations in December. Elon Musk then replied "No" on X to a post asking about December ordering.

Why it is being discussed: The two posts moved fast. By the morning of 31 October, Musk's reply had about 264,000 views and more than 3,200 likes, and the reporter's post had about 228,000 views, according to X's public metrics. X also featured the dispute in a trending story. A reservation date would be the first sign of when buyers could actually get an Optimus.
What to watch: Whether Tesla itself announces anything about reservations or pricing, and whether Optimus V3 appears at The Humanoids Summit in December, as the Standard reported was planned.
analysis: Opinion: Until Tesla publishes its own ordering details, both the December date and the price expectation should be treated as unverified. A one-word reply to a joking post is not a full rebuttal either, which is why this story is likely to keep circulating until the company says more.

title: Lightberry's Lumi humanoid gets a US Conditional Approval and is exempted from the FCC Covered List
seo_title: Lightberry Lumi gets FCC Covered List exemption
summary: An FCC notice on 30 October exempted Lightberry's Lumi robots from the Covered List after a Department of War approval tied to an onshoring plan.
body: Short answer: On 30 October 2026, the US Federal Communications Commission issued Public Notice DA 26-1181, which exempts Lightberry Holdings' "Lumi Interactive mobile robots" from the FCC Covered List after the Department of War (DoW) granted them a Conditional Approval. San Francisco start-up Lightberry says this clears the way for it to market and sell Lumi in the United States, according to its announcement.

According to Lightberry, the FCC on 28 July 2026 added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to the Covered List, except those granted a Conditional Approval by the DoW, and devices on that list cannot receive the FCC authorisation needed to be imported, marketed or sold in the US. The FCC notice says a Conditional Approval is "a specific determination" by the DoW that the devices do not pose risks to US national security.

The exemption comes with conditions. The FCC notice says it depends on each company's continued compliance with the onshoring plan in its application and on updated vetting of its products. A footnote adds that failing to follow the plan, or a false statement in the application, could end the approval and put the equipment back on the Covered List. Lightberry says its plan includes replacing the robot's sensors, onboard computer and software with its own, and starting US manufacturing with the body, head and hands.

Lightberry says Lumi is about 127 cm tall and designed for businesses, where it can hold conversations, guide visitors, tell stories and take photos. The company says Lumi is compatible with the Unitree G1, and that a Founder Edition priced at $39,990 will ship in 2026. Lightberry was founded in 2025 by chief executive Ali Attar and Stephan Koenigstorfer, according to the announcement, and it describes itself as the first and only American humanoid robot company cleared by the US government.

The same notice also lists approvals for warehouse and industrial robots from ARAPL, ATI Motors, SunScout, Swap Robotics and OMRON, a drone from Voliro and power inverters from Ingeteam. For more on US policy toward robot imports, see our story on the Section 232 robotics review and our funding and policy hub.
analysis: Opinion: This notice shows what the Covered List route looks like in practice for humanoids built on foreign hardware. Approval is not a blanket pass. It is tied to an onshoring plan and ongoing checks, so the real milestone for Lightberry will be shipping robots with its own sensors, computer and US-made parts.
disclaimer: This article summarises a US government notice and a company announcement for general information only. It is not legal, regulatory, trade or investment advice; consult a qualified adviser about your own situation. Product details and prices are as stated by Lightberry.

title: SynDexy delivers its first small batch of C1 dexterous humanoids for precision assembly
seo_title: SynDexy C1 humanoid first small batch delivery
summary: Beijing start-up SynDexy says its C1, a wheeled two-arm humanoid with vision and touch sensing, has shipped in a first small batch for factory assembly.
body: Short answer: SynDexy, a Beijing robotics start-up founded in 2025, announced on 30 October 2026 that it has delivered its first small batch of C1 humanoid robots, a wheeled design with two arms built for precision assembly work in consumer electronics and component factories, according to Pandaily. The company has not said how many units it delivered or who the customers are, Pandaily reported.

The C1's main selling point is touch. According to Gasgoo, SynDexy developed its own visuotactile sensors, which it says reach micron-level spatial resolution, and pairs them with an in-house model called M1 that combines vision, touch and force. The company says this lets the robot handle fine, contact-heavy steps such as assembling flexible circuits and inserting cables.

SynDexy lists 22 degrees of freedom for the C1 and a motion control cycle of 1 millisecond, and says the robot reached a success rate above 98% on key tasks in earlier testing, according to both reports. These are company figures that have not been independently tested, and Pandaily notes that SynDexy has not backed its description of M1 as a first of its kind with outside comparisons. Both outlets say development began in April 2026, with a prototype in July and the first batch in October.

According to Pandaily, the company's chief scientist is Professor Fang Bin of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, and its team includes people from Tsinghua University, Beihang University, Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Huawei, DJI and Tencent, with researchers making up more than 90% of staff. For more on touch sensing for robots, see our story on MoSense's electronic skin, and find more Chinese humanoid news on our China hub and deployments hub.
analysis: Opinion: Fine assembly is one of the hardest jobs to automate, which is why touch sensing is drawing so much attention. A first batch with no named customers or unit count is an early step, and the success rate will matter most once it is reported from real production lines.

title: Researchers teach a Unitree G1 with a 20-joint hand to catch objects it never saw in training
seo_title: Catch It All: Unitree G1 learns to catch unseen objects
summary: A UC San Diego team trained a seated Unitree G1 in simulation to catch thrown objects using one head camera, succeeding in over a third of real tosses.
body: Short answer: Researchers from UC San Diego and Harvey Mudd College have trained a seated Unitree G1 humanoid to catch thrown objects underhand and overhand using only one camera on its head, according to a paper titled Catch It All! posted to arXiv on 28 October 2026. The policies were trained only in simulation and then run on the real robot without extra tuning, and they caught 9 everyday objects that were never used in training.

In real tests, the robot caught objects in 38.9% of underhand tosses and 36.1% of overhand tosses, according to the paper. The test objects included plush toys, a sandbag, a squashable bag of chips and rigid toys that bounce, and each was thrown at short, medium and long range. For comparison, the authors say a human teleoperator using a two-arm control rig caught only 3 of 44 tosses, which they give as the reason for training with reinforcement learning in simulation instead of learning from demonstrations.

According to the paper and the project page, the setup uses a 20-joint House of Dextra hand, a ZED 2i stereo camera mounted on the robot's head and an object tracker called SAM2-Tiny. The team says the key ideas were a reward that pulls every fingertip toward the object's surface and training schedules that keep the arm within its limits. The authors say these safety-aware schedules let the policy act quickly close to hardware limits, including wrist torque limits as low as 5 newton metres.

The authors say they have not yet applied the method to whole-body control and plan to do so next. The project page links to a public code repository. For more research on the same robot family, visit our Unitree hub and research hub, and for another take on robot hands see our story on Samsung's five-finger hands.
analysis: Opinion: A success rate under 40% will not impress anyone looking for a factory-ready skill, but catching unfamiliar objects from a single moving camera is a hard test of fast perception and control. The more lasting lesson may be the focus on staying within the torque limits of a light humanoid arm.

title: Electric vs hydraulic actuators: why humanoid robots moved to electric joints
seo_title: Electric vs hydraulic actuators in humanoid robots
summary: Hydraulic joints gave early humanoids huge power in a small package. Electric actuators won out because they are quieter, cleaner, easier to control and simpler to build at scale.
body: Short answer: An actuator is the part that makes a robot joint move. Hydraulic actuators push pressurised fluid through cylinders and can deliver very high force for their size. Electric actuators use a motor, usually paired with a gearbox or screw, and are cleaner, quieter and easier to control precisely. Most humanoids being built for factories today use electric joints, and the most famous hydraulic humanoid was retired in 2024.

How hydraulics work. A pump pressurises fluid, valves route it, and pistons convert the pressure into motion. The big advantage is power density: a compact cylinder can produce enough force for jumps, flips and fast recoveries. The costs are a pump, hoses, seals and fluid that can leak, plus noise and heat. Every joint depends on a pressurised system that needs regular maintenance.

How electric actuators work. A motor spins quickly with modest torque, so designers add a reduction stage to trade speed for force. Common choices are planetary gearboxes, harmonic or strain wave drives, and roller screws for linear joints such as knees. Sensors on the motor and output let software control position, speed and torque closely. A joint built this way is sealed and quiet, and it runs from the same battery as the computer.

The Atlas switch. Boston Dynamics spent more than a decade showing what its hydraulic Atlas could do, including parkour and backflips. In April 2024 it announced the retirement of the hydraulic Atlas and unveiled a fully electric Atlas designed for real world applications, with Hyundai's manufacturing operations as the first testing ground. The company framed the change as part of moving from research to a commercial product.

Why electric won for factory work. Factory customers care about uptime, safety around people and cost per unit. Electric joints can be made as repeatable modules, which is why suppliers now sell humanoid joint modules as products. Schaeffler, for example, says its Taicang factory in China assembles joint modules, including actuators, for humanoid robots, as we reported in October. Hydraulic systems are harder to standardise this way.

Where hydraulics still make sense. Very heavy machines, construction equipment and some legged research platforms still use hydraulics because nothing else delivers as much force in a small space. The trade off is complexity, and for a robot meant to work beside people all day, most makers have decided that trade is not worth it.

title: How much does a humanoid robot cost in 2026? Prices compared
seo_title: Humanoid robot prices compared (2026): Unitree, 1X, AGIBOT
summary: Unitree lists G1 from $13,500, H2 at $29,900; 1X prices NEO at $20,000 or $499/month. Figure, Tesla and Apptronik have published no price.
body: Short answer: As of 2 November 2026, most humanoid makers still do not sell their robots like an ordinary product with a public price tag. Three do: Unitree lists its G1 from $13,500 and its full-size H2 at $29,900, both before tax and shipping, on its own product pages. 1X prices its NEO home robot at $20,000 to own, with a 3-year warranty, or $499 a month to subscribe, on its order page. AGIBOT's international store lists the A2 Lite, a performance and interaction humanoid, at $44,560. Figure, Tesla and Apptronik have not published a sale price for their flagship humanoids; each is still shipping only to enterprise partners or talking about where a price might land once production scales up.

Unitree's own product pages set its numbers. The G1, the company's smaller research and development platform, is listed from $13,500, tax and shipping excluded; a higher-spec G1 EDU variant is listed as 'Contact Sales' rather than a fixed price. The larger H2, about 1.8 metres tall, is listed at $29,900 on the same terms, with the H2 EDU variant again priced on request. We previously compared the H2's roughly 3-hour battery life with other makers' runtimes in our runtime report; more Unitree coverage is on our Unitree hub.

1X takes a different approach. Its order page prices the NEO at $20,000 for outright ownership, which it says includes a 3-year warranty and priority delivery, or $499 a month as a subscription with standard delivery. The same page says US deliveries start in 2026, without giving an exact date, and lists NEO's runtime at 4 hours per charge.

AGIBOT, based in Shanghai, sells several humanoids directly through its international online store. The A2 Lite, aimed at entertainment and commercial performance work such as group dance routines and tai chi demonstrations, has a listed sale price of $44,560, plus $500 to $3,000 in shipping and any import duties the buyer owes locally. The more capable A2 Ultra, which adds navigation, object recognition and an interactive screen, is priced on request rather than listed outright. More Chinese humanoid coverage is on our China hub.

Figure has not published a price for either of its current humanoids. Its October 2025 announcement introducing the Figure 03, designed for homes as well as factories, describes the robot's hardware and manufacturing in detail but states no price, and the Figure 04, whose design Figure says is now locked, has no published specifications or price either, as covered in our Figure 04 report. Figure 03 units have gone only to the company's own programs and to enterprise partners such as carmakers, not to a public order page.

Tesla has never published a retail price or an order page for Optimus. The only figure Elon Musk has given in public remains the one from Tesla's We, Robot event on 10 October 2024, where he said the robot should eventually cost 'probably $20,000-$30,000 long term,' according to CNBC's report of the event. Musk told Tesla's Q3 2026 earnings call that Optimus is moving into early production on the company's Fremont line, but set an end-2027 target for deliveries to outside customers rather than a price, as we reported in our deliveries target article.

Apptronik has not published a price for Apollo either. Co-founder and chief executive Jeff Cardenas told IEEE Spectrum in 2023, when Apollo was introduced, that a humanoid should eventually cost less than $50,000, comparable to the price of a car; that was a long-term goal stated before the robot had shipped to any customer, not a current price. Apollo today is deployed only through enterprise pilot and development agreements with manufacturing and logistics partners, not sold against a published price list. Agility Robotics follows a similar pattern: it does not sell Digit directly either, instead reaching customers such as GXO and AGCO through its own agreements, which we track on our Agility Robotics hub, deployments hub and deployment tracker.

The pattern across these companies splits in two: Unitree, 1X and AGIBOT publish a number a buyer can act on today, while Figure, Tesla, Apptronik and Agility either have no price or only a long-term aim. AiMOGA's Mobo, a home companion robot that opened worldwide pre-orders in October, falls into the same no-price-yet group. A published list price is also not the same as being able to buy a robot today: several of the companies above still restrict sales to approved customers or specific countries. For the wider funding and policy picture around these companies, see our funding and policy hub.
analysis: Opinion: A public price is becoming as much of a dividing line in humanoid robotics as any spec sheet. Unitree, 1X and AGIBOT are selling machines that a business, or in 1X's case a household, can order today, which lets outside buyers compare them like any other piece of equipment. Figure, Tesla and Apptronik, each backed by large funding rounds, are still choosing to grow through direct enterprise deals and distant cost targets instead. That may be the steadier path while the hardware and software mature, but it also means a reader cannot yet compare the $13,500 G1 with a future Optimus on equal terms: one is a number, the other is a prediction, and the two are not the same thing to weigh against each other.

title: Robots take on Mount Tai's 3,100 stone steps: what the CMG challenge tested
seo_title: CMG World Robot Mount Tai Challenge: humanoids climb 3,100 steps
summary: Nearly 90 teams sent humanoid, quadruped and exoskeleton robots up a Mount Tai stone path on 2 November, according to Euronews and AFP.
body: Short answer: On Monday, 2 November 2026, nearly 90 teams took part in the CMG World Robot Mount Tai Challenge in Tai'an, Shandong Province, according to Euronews. Humanoid, quadruped and exoskeleton robots climbed a 3.9 km stretch of the mountain's ancient path, with about 3,100 stone steps and roughly 600 metres of elevation gain. According to AFP's report carried by CBS News, the fastest humanoid, from the Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue, finished a shorter humanoid course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds, while a four-legged robot from Beijing Lingyi Technology, a Unitree subsidiary, won the quadruped speed category in 43 minutes and 41 seconds.

Mount Tai is one of China's best-known mountains, and its main walking route is a long staircase of uneven, worn stone. Euronews describes the course as a mix of steep slopes, long stairways and sharp bends. That is very different from the flat floors of a factory, a warehouse or a showroom, where most humanoid demonstrations take place.

The organisers framed the event as a real-world endurance test. Teams could enter in different ways, according to the AFP report: some tried to complete the route as fast as possible, while others had to carry fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit. Euronews adds that some quadruped robots carried food supplies along the track. Local media quoted organisers calling the rocky terrain a natural extreme testing ground that could help prepare robots for real-world use.

For scale, CCTV said most tourists take at least two hours to walk the route, according to the AFP report. The winning quadruped's time of under 44 minutes on the full course is therefore well ahead of a typical hiker. The humanoid result is not directly comparable, because the fastest humanoid ran a shorter course than the full route, and the reports we reviewed do not give that course's exact length.

Why stairs are hard for humanoids. Walking up stone steps forces a two-legged robot to place each foot precisely on surfaces that vary in height, depth and grip, while keeping its centre of mass over a small support area. Any slip has to be caught within a fraction of a second. Steps that are chipped, sloped or wet add uncertainty the robot's sensors and controller must handle continuously. A long climb also strains batteries and joint motors, which heat up under sustained load, so a course like this tests endurance as well as balance.

Four-legged robots have a natural advantage here. With more feet on the ground at once, they are statically more stable, and their lower bodies make falls less damaging. That helps explain why the quadruped category could run the full route while the fastest humanoid result came on a shorter course.

Who took part. According to Euronews, the field covered three kinds of machines: humanoids, quadrupeds and exoskeletons, the wearable frames that assist a human walker. The reports we reviewed name only the two category winners mentioned above; they do not list full results, finishing rates or how much human help each robot received. Engineers walked alongside the machines, according to the AFP coverage, which is normal practice for safety at events like this.

What the event shows and what it does not. Public challenges like this give a rare look at how robots behave outside controlled labs, and the stair-climbing format is a clear, easy-to-understand test. But a single race does not show how often a robot completes such a course, how much remote control or intervention was used, or whether the same machines could do useful work at the top. Those details were not published in the reports we reviewed, so the results are best read as a demonstration rather than a benchmark.
For more on the companies involved in this sector, see our Unitree hub.
analysis: Endurance events on natural terrain are likely to become more common because they are easy for the public to follow and hard to fake on video. For buyers, though, what matters is repeatable performance under supervision rules that are published in advance. We would watch for organisers releasing full results, intervention counts and course lengths, which would make future editions far more useful as a comparison between makers.

title: Xiaomi Puts Two Humanoids Through an Eight-Hour Auto-Parts Sorting Trial
summary: Xiaomi’s latest factory video extends its humanoid testing to an eight-hour component-sorting task, while leaving key productivity and autonomy figures undisclosed.
body: Xiaomi has released a November 3 video showing two humanoid robots sorting center-console side covers at its automotive factory. The company describes the exercise as an eight-hour task, a more demanding test of continuity than a short promotional clip of a robot lifting a single component. The robots are shown moving parts between mobile containers and upright racks with individual slots, according to Humanoids Daily’s account of the company footage.

The distinction between performing a movement and completing a factory assignment matters. A sorting station requires a machine to recognize which component belongs where, pick it without damaging the surface, position it correctly, and avoid disrupting the flow of parts to downstream assembly. The physical surroundings also matter: the robots are not operating on an empty stage but beside racks and carts resembling the equipment a human worker would encounter in a production area.

Xiaomi says the system detects and corrects anomalies autonomously and coordinates with its production-line systems. Those are company claims, not independently established performance measurements. The published material does not specify what counted as an anomaly, how many incidents occurred, or whether an operator had to intervene during the run. The video uses accelerated playback, including labels for five-times and 100-times speed, and a cumulative working-time counter. Such presentation can show task variety and continuity without documenting every minute of an entire shift.

This is not Xiaomi’s first attempt to put humanoid technology near vehicle manufacturing. In March, the company reported a 90.2% success rate during a three-hour autonomous pilot involving simultaneous installation of self-tapping nuts on both sides of an assembly, while meeting a 76-second production-cycle requirement. That result concerns a different operation; it cannot be carried over as the accuracy rate for the November side-cover exercise. In April, Xiaomi also showed CyberOne V2 interacting with visitors and distributing gift bags at an investor event, a setting with different safety and reliability demands.

The latest trial therefore advances one specific claim: Xiaomi is testing whether its robots can repeat a comparatively narrow parts-handling routine over a working-shift-length period. It does not yet establish that the robots outperform a fixed industrial arm, cost less than a conventional sorting station, or can transfer without retraining to a different vehicle component. Those are separate questions for a purchasing manager considering a deployment.

A factory operator would want to know the number of covers processed per hour, the fraction placed correctly on the first attempt, the time spent recovering from mistakes, and the extent of human supervision. Battery information is another gap. Eight hours of elapsed activity is not evidence of eight hours on a single charge; the company has not disclosed whether charging breaks or battery swaps were involved.

The commercial opportunity is nonetheless intelligible. Automotive factories handle many parts whose shapes, packaging and delivery schedules change across models. A mobile, general-purpose robot might eventually be redeployed among several such stations rather than engineered for one fixed task. That flexibility has economic value only if changeovers, error rates and maintenance remain manageable.

Xiaomi’s November footage is best read as a demonstration of sustained task testing, not proof of a fully staffed-out robotic production line. The next consequential update would be an independently auditable shift report: actual throughput, intervention counts and uptime, compared with the existing human or automated process. Until then, the company has shown a promising application and identified precisely the measurements it still needs to publish.

title: Figure 03 Robots Leave BotQ on Foot, but Production Scale Remains Unclear
summary: A new video from Figure CEO Brett Adcock shows completed humanoids walking out of BotQ, without disclosing current output or customer deliveries.
body: Figure founder and chief executive Brett Adcock posted a roughly 19-second video on November 2 showing newly manufactured Figure 03 humanoids walking outside the company’s BotQ manufacturing facility. Several white-and-black robots move along a building approach and toward a marked pedestrian crossing, with people nearby. Adcock described them as heading across campus after leaving BotQ, according to Humanoids Daily.

The images are a useful snapshot of physical output, but they answer fewer business questions than their visual impact might suggest. The post gives no current weekly production rate, number of units completed in the latest batch, customer shipment total or breakdown between research and commercial use. Nor does the video establish whether the walking sequence was fully autonomous, supervised remotely or run under another control arrangement.

Those distinctions are especially important for a company positioning humanoids as a scalable workforce technology. A robot that walks from a factory building is a manufactured unit; it is not necessarily an installed, revenue-generating machine. Factory output, delivery, acceptance testing and paid deployment are separate milestones, and counting them interchangeably would inflate the commercial significance of a campus clip.

Figure has previously supplied more concrete markers. In April, Adcock said BotQ had produced more robots in March than over the company’s entire prior history, although he did not provide a unit count in that update. In July, the company celebrated production of its 1,000th Figure 03 with a gold-colored unit and a team photograph. That was a cumulative manufacturing milestone rather than a statement that 1,000 units had been delivered to buyers. The November footage adds evidence that machines continue to emerge from BotQ but no updated cumulative figure.

The reason manufacturing matters goes beyond sales. Figure develops its own robot-control AI, Helix, and a larger internal fleet can provide more opportunities to collect manipulation and navigation examples, test component durability, and expose failure modes that do not appear in a single demonstration. Even robots retained on campus can contribute to development, although the value of that data depends on how varied and representative their tasks are.

Figure’s reported commercial and pilot activity has included work with BMW Manufacturing and retail group Catalyst Brands. Those relationships provide possible environments for testing whether robots can handle the repetition, interruptions and safety requirements of real workplaces. But the November walking footage is not itself a new announcement about either customer. It does not identify the destinations of the robots shown.

The company also faces the problem of model turnover. While Figure 03 units are leaving BotQ, Figure is developing Figure 04, which could alter the economics of tooling, spare parts, servicing and customer adoption. Manufacturers often need to stabilize a design long enough to build it repeatedly, even while engineering teams prepare the next generation. A rapid succession of prototypes can impress observers without producing a predictable delivery schedule.

For prospective customers, the relevant follow-up disclosures would include completed robots per month, how many pass final acceptance tests, how many reach external sites, and what work they perform after installation. For investors, the same figures would help distinguish capital-intensive fleet building from recurring commercial demand.

The new video does demonstrate something concrete: multiple newly completed humanoids moving through an ordinary outdoor campus setting. It should not be promoted as a new sales record or evidence of mass deployment. Figure’s manufacturing story will become much easier to evaluate when the company pairs visible robots with comparable production and field-performance data.

title: AGIBOT Tests Six G2 Robots in a 24-Hour Convenience Store Broadcast
summary: AGIBOT’s November 2–3 livestream puts six G2 humanoids into a store setting to demonstrate varied service tasks, though uninterrupted autonomy has not been established.
body: Chinese robotics developer AGIBOT staged a 24-hour convenience-store demonstration spanning November 2 and November 3, putting six G2 robots in a setting designed to resemble a demanding retail shift. The company called the event “Robots Never Clock Out.” Humanoids Daily reported that the broadcast began at 10 a.m. China time on November 2 and was scheduled to end at 10 a.m. on November 3, equivalent to 02:00 UTC on each date.

The announced tasks were deliberately broader than the single pick-and-place motions common in robotics clips. AGIBOT planned to show the robots stocking shelves, making coffee, preparing hot food, greeting customers and removing rubbish. It described the machines as store trainees encountering rush-hour traffic, overnight duty and the breakfast period. Those are different operational conditions, with changing human activity and demands on the robots’ hands, navigation and task planning.

A convenience store is a revealing choice of environment. Unlike a structured assembly station, a shop contains customers who move unpredictably, products that vary in size and packaging, and tasks that may be interrupted. A machine must avoid collisions, preserve food-handling hygiene, identify the correct item and return to unfinished work after a disruption. A robot that can make coffee in isolation may still struggle to do so while other machines and people share the counter.

A full-day livestream provides more context than a polished 20-second demonstration. Viewers can observe transitions between tasks and the physical space over time. But the length of a broadcast should not be confused with each robot working autonomously for 24 consecutive hours. The published description does not provide a verified per-robot duty cycle, human-assistance log, charging record or count of completed orders. Six robots sharing a shift could rotate through duties and maintenance periods.

That missing information is central to the economics. A retailer evaluating such a system would compare the number of orders or stocking tasks completed, time per task, breakage, customer wait times and safety incidents against an existing operation. It would also ask how many employees must supervise the machines. A deployment that replaces one repetitive task but requires constant specialist oversight could still be valuable as research, yet fall short of an immediate labor-saving proposition.

The food-preparation elements raise additional issues. Preparing hot food requires temperature and handling safeguards beyond those needed to move boxed goods. Coffee preparation involves liquids, heat and cleanup. The demonstration’s task list is evidence of what AGIBOT intended to test, not certification that the system satisfies food-safety rules or can be left unsupervised in a commercial store.

The G2 challenge also shows how robotics marketing is changing. Developers increasingly seek to prove endurance, multitasking and interaction in a recognizable workplace rather than just athletic motion. The store format allows AGIBOT to present many robot capabilities in a single event, while also creating an opportunity for outsiders to ask whether the same capabilities would persist during unplanned interruptions.

For a meaningful independent assessment, AGIBOT could publish an event log showing each robot’s active minutes, tasks attempted, successful completions, remote interventions, charging periods and safety stops. Video archives alone may not reveal every off-camera intervention. Such a report would convert a promotional demonstration into a benchmark that other vendors and prospective customers could compare.

The November event is a substantive attempt to test multiple humanoids in a shared service environment. Its strongest verified fact is the six-robot, 24-hour public challenge and the work categories announced. Claims about continuous autonomous retail operation require additional evidence that the broadcast description does not yet supply.

title: LiberAI's Liber-0 Completes 36% of Unseen Robot Tasks Zero-Shot
summary: LiberAI says its Liber-0 world action model, pretrained on 2.2 million hours of human experience, succeeded in 36% of trials on 60 tasks it was not trained for.
body: Robotics start-up LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a "world action model" that it says can carry out manipulation tasks a robot was never shown how to do. The company announced it on X: "Introducing Liber-0, our World Action Model for zero-shot robot manipulation—including dexterous, multi-step tasks."

According to LiberAI's announcement on ACCESS Newswire, Liber-0 achieved a 36.0% overall success rate across 600 trials covering 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6, without training on robot demonstrations collected for those tasks. The model did see robot data during pretraining, which is why LiberAI calls this "task-level" zero-shot generalisation.

How the tests broke down. The 60 tasks were split into three groups of 20, each tried 10 times. Liber-0 succeeded 63.5% of the time on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on the second group of short manipulation tasks and 10.5% on the hardest group of long, multi-step tasks, the company said.

For comparison, LiberAI's technical blog reports testing GPT-6 Astra on its own as a robot controller on the same tasks, over 180 trials. It scored 8.3% on pick-and-place and 5.0% on short non-pick-and-place tasks, and LiberAI says it struggled with contact-rich work that needs precise hand control. These are LiberAI's own results and have not been independently reproduced.

Learning from people, not robots. Liber-0 is pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. To turn human video into actions a robot can copy, LiberAI records hand motion with its LiberSense Glove, which the blog says is 0.3 mm thick and weighs 131 g. Its LEO robot platform uses dexterous hands, articulated wrists and a waist, with cameras placed to match how the human data was filmed. A shared "embodiment representation" tells the model about the body it is controlling.

LiberAI says glove recordings scaled better than far larger amounts of web video in its tests, and that mixing them with limited robot data beat robot-only training while using 75% fewer robot demonstrations. For multi-step jobs, Liber-0 can optionally pair with a reasoning model such as GPT-6 Astra to plan intermediate goals.

Robotics & Automation News also covered the launch. A 36% success rate is far from deployment-ready, but it suggests human recordings could cut the cost of teaching robots each new task one demonstration at a time.
