title: South Korea Opens First AI Humanoid Data Factory at KIMM to Train Robots for Real-World Tasks
summary: South Korea has opened its first dedicated facility for producing training data for bipedal humanoid robots, placing hands-on robot learning at the center...
body: South Korea has opened its first dedicated facility for producing training data for bipedal humanoid robots, placing hands-on robot learning at the center of its push to develop domestic artificial intelligence technology. The AI Humanoid Data Factory, unveiled on November 3 at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM), is intended to help robots learn tasks they may eventually perform without human operators, according to Aju Press.

Built in collaboration with the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI), the facility occupies approximately 1,000 square meters across two floors of a KIMM building. It currently operates 12 humanoid robots, with plans to increase that number to 25. Its focus is not mass-producing finished robots, but systematically gathering the physical task data needed to train their AI systems.

From Remote Operation to Robot Learning. At the opening ceremony, researchers remotely guided humanoids through a range of practical activities. The robots retrieved items from a refrigerator, handled laundry, straightened a sofa and operated buttons and levers inside a vehicle. These demonstrations illustrated the variety of movements and interactions that the facility is designed to capture, Aju Press reported.

The process begins with human-directed movement. As an operator controls a robot, the system records what the robot does while completing a task. Those records are then used to train vision-language-action models, which connect visual information and instructions with physical actions.

Importantly, the process does not end once a model has been trained. KIMM puts the trained AI back into robots to evaluate its performance, then uses information from those tests in subsequent training. This feedback loop is designed to improve how robots translate learned behavior into movement in the physical world.

The opening demonstrations therefore should not be confused with proof that the robots can already complete every displayed task autonomously. Remote operation is part of how the factory creates the examples that future autonomous systems can learn from.

KAIROS and a Domestic Humanoid Platform. KIMM also demonstrated KAIROS, its homegrown humanoid development project. At the November 3 event, KAIROS showed precise object manipulation and the ability to imitate full-body human movements. The institute began developing the robot a little more than a year ago, and the first version is scheduled for April 2027, according to Aju Press.

The new factory is expected to serve a broader purpose than improving a single machine. KIMM plans to open access in stages to outside companies, universities and research institutions beginning in late 2027. That timetable would allow other organizations to participate in the data infrastructure being assembled at the institute.

KIMM also expects domestic data collection to reduce reliance on foreign training datasets and AI models. This makes the facility part of a wider effort to build technological capacity within South Korea rather than depend entirely on tools developed elsewhere.

Part of a Larger National Investment. The project receives support from South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT through K-Moonshot, a national initiative applying AI to 12 missions, including humanoid robotics. The ministry is targeting a world-class national humanoid platform within three years, while its Next-X Humanoid Challenge is scheduled to begin making final selections from 2027.

The factory's opening follows a larger funding commitment. On August 27, the Ministry of Planning and Budget earmarked 2.3 trillion won, approximately $1.7 billion, for the humanoid industry through 2030. The plan includes purchases of 1,080 domestically produced humanoids and a goal of increasing the domestic share of essential components from roughly 45% to 80%, Aju Press reported.

Together, those measures connect data collection, robot development and domestic manufacturing. The immediate milestone is a working facility with 12 robots collecting examples of physical tasks. The longer-term test will be whether that expanding body of training data helps South Korean humanoids perform useful work with less direct human control.

title: What is a vision-language-action model? How robots turn words into movement
seo_title: Vision-language-action (VLA) models explained
summary: A VLA model takes camera images and an instruction and outputs robot actions. RT-2, Gemini Robotics, pi0 and Figure's Helix are the best-known examples.
body: Short answer: A vision-language-action (VLA) model is an AI model that looks at camera images, reads an instruction such as "put the apple in the bowl", and outputs the motor commands a robot needs to do it. Most VLAs start from a vision-language model trained on web images and text, then learn actions from robot data. Google DeepMind's RT-2, Gemini Robotics, Physical Intelligence's pi0 and Figure's Helix are the best-known published examples.

Where the idea came from. Google DeepMind described RT-2 on 28 July 2023 as a VLA that learns from both web and robotics data. It was built on existing vision-language models (PaLI-X and PaLM-E) and trained with robot demonstrations that DeepMind says were collected with 13 robots over 17 months in an office kitchen. The trick, according to DeepMind, was to represent robot actions as tokens in the model's output, the same way a language model outputs words.

Why it matters. A model that has learned from the web already knows what an apple, a drawer or a recycling bin is. DeepMind says RT-2 could follow commands it had not seen in its robot data and do basic reasoning, such as picking a rock as an improvised hammer. That is the main promise of VLAs: fewer hand-programmed skills and fewer demonstrations per task.

Different designs. Physical Intelligence said on 31 October 2024 that its pi0 model starts from a 3-billion-parameter vision-language model and adds continuous action outputs through flow matching, a variant of diffusion models, so it can send motor commands up to 50 times a second. Figure's Helix, announced on 20 February 2025, splits the job in two: a slower onboard vision-language model running at 7 to 9 Hz for understanding, and a fast visuomotor policy that outputs actions at 200 Hz. Figure says Helix controls the whole humanoid upper body, including individual fingers, and runs on embedded GPUs on the robot. NVIDIA's open GR00T models use a similar "System 1, System 2" split; see our GR00T explainer.

Gemini Robotics. On 12 March 2025 Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics, a VLA built on Gemini 2.0 with physical actions added as an output, and Gemini Robotics-ER for spatial reasoning. DeepMind said it was partnering with Apptronik to build humanoid robots with Gemini 2.0, and that Gemini Robotics more than doubled performance on its generalisation benchmark compared with other state-of-the-art VLAs, by its own measure.

What VLAs still need. Every one of these models is trained partly on robot demonstrations, which are slow and costly to collect. Figure says Helix used about 500 hours of teleoperated data. Companies gather that data with remote human operators and add simulated data; NVIDIA's approach is in our GR00T explainer.
analysis: Analysis: "VLA" has become a catch-all label, and the published designs differ a lot in speed, size and how actions are produced. The useful question for any new announcement is what the model controls (a gripper, two arms, a whole body), how fast it runs, and whether it runs on the robot or in the cloud. Benchmark claims so far are mostly companies grading their own models.
disclaimer: Performance claims are the developers' own statements from their announcements and have not been independently verified.

title: Boston Dynamics' electric Atlas explained: specs, battery swaps and Hyundai
seo_title: Boston Dynamics electric Atlas: specs and what it does
summary: Boston Dynamics retired hydraulic Atlas in April 2024. The electric Atlas lists 56 degrees of freedom, a 4-hour battery it swaps itself and a 50 kg lift.
body: Short answer: Atlas is Boston Dynamics' humanoid robot. In April 2024 the company retired the hydraulic Atlas famous for parkour videos and unveiled a fully electric Atlas designed for real work, starting with its owner Hyundai's car plants. Boston Dynamics now markets Atlas as an enterprise industrial humanoid for material handling, and lists a 4-hour battery that the robot swaps itself, 56 degrees of freedom and a lift of up to 50 kg.

Hydraulic to electric. In its April 2024 blog post Boston Dynamics said the electric Atlas would be stronger and have a broader range of motion than any previous generation, and that it would test applications with a small group of customers, beginning with Hyundai, over the following few years. Why the industry has moved to electric joints is covered in our actuators explainer.

Published specs. On its Atlas product page Boston Dynamics lists a height of 1.9 m (6.2 ft) and weight of 90 kg (198 lb), plus: battery life of 4 hours; weight capacity of 50 kg (110 lb) instantaneous and 30 kg (66 lb) sustained; 56 degrees of freedom; a reach of 2.3 m (7.5 ft); and continuous range of motion in its joints. Those are the company's own figures. Unitree's published joint counts are in Unitree G1 vs H1.

Working without stopping. Boston Dynamics says Atlas autonomously walks to a charging station and swaps out its own battery before returning to work. It also says Atlas needs minimal supervision for material handling, supports barcode scanning and workflow integrations, and connects to factory and warehouse systems through its Orbit software. When one Atlas learns a skill, the company says it can be deployed across the fleet.
How it compares. For context on battery life across makers, see published humanoid runtimes. Boston Dynamics has not published a price for Atlas; our price comparison lists the makers that have.

title: Unitree G1 vs H1 vs H1-2: humanoid specs compared
seo_title: Unitree G1 vs H1 vs H1-2 specs compared
summary: Unitree's G1 is a 1.32 m, 35 kg robot with 23 to 43 degrees of freedom; the H1 is about 1.8 m and 47 kg; the H1-2 is about 1.78 m, 70 kg.
body: Short answer: Unitree sells humanoids in two sizes. The G1 is a compact robot about 1.32 metres tall and about 35 kg, with 23 degrees of freedom in the base model and up to 43 in the G1 EDU. The full-size H1 is about 1.8 metres and 47 kg, and the newer H1-2 is about 1.78 metres and 70 kg with 27 degrees of freedom. All figures below are from Unitree's own product pages.

Unitree G1. Unitree lists the G1 at 1320 x 450 x 200 mm standing, folding to 690 x 450 x 300 mm. Each leg has 6 degrees of freedom, the waist 1 (the EDU can add 2 more), and each arm 5. The EDU adds optional three-fingered Dex3-1 hands with 7 degrees of freedom each, 2 optional extra wrist joints, with tactile sensor arrays as an option. Maximum knee torque is listed as 90 N·m (120 N·m on the EDU) and arm load at about 2 kg (about 3 kg on the EDU). It senses with a depth camera and 3D LiDAR, and runs on an 8-core CPU.

Unitree H1. The H1 is listed at about 180 cm and about 47 kg, with a moving speed of 3.3 m/s, an 864 Wh quickly replaceable battery, peak torque density of 189 N·m/kg and maximum joint torque of 360 N·m.

Unitree H1-2. The H1-2 is about 178 cm and about 70 kg with 27 degrees of freedom in total, four more than the base G1. Unitree lists maximum arm joint torque of 120 N·m and leg joint torque of 360 N·m.

Which is which. The G1 is the cheaper, smaller research and education platform, and the robot most often seen in university demos and competitions. The H series is full human size. Unitree's newer H2 and its published prices are in our price comparison, and battery life in published runtimes. All Unitree coverage is on our Unitree hub.

Reading the numbers. Degrees of freedom count the robot's independently driven joints; more joints usually means more dexterity but more cost and complexity. Boston Dynamics lists 56 for the electric Atlas; see electric Atlas explained.

title: 1X NEO explained: price, Expert Mode and how the home robot works
seo_title: 1X NEO home robot: price and how it works
summary: 1X sells NEO for $20,000 or $499 a month, with a $200 deposit and US deliveries from 2026. It uses Redwood AI plus remote expert help for new chores.
body: Short answer: NEO is a humanoid robot for the home made by 1X. On its order page 1X lists NEO at $20,000 to own, with a 3-year warranty, or $499 a month on a subscription, with a fully refundable $200 deposit and US deliveries starting in 2026. 1X says NEO arrives with basic autonomy and learns more over time, and that for chores it cannot yet do, a 1X expert can remotely supervise it at scheduled times.

The AI. 1X says NEO uses Redwood AI, which it calls its generalist AI model, to learn and repeat tasks, alongside a built-in large language model for conversation. Owners can talk to NEO by voice, manage a chore schedule in the NEO app, and pilot it remotely through the app or a VR device, according to the product page.

Expert Mode. This is the feature that draws the most questions. 1X describes a Scheduled Expert Mode in which, for complex tasks NEO does not know, an expert from 1X remotely supervises its actions to help it learn and get the job done. In practice that means a person at 1X may be operating or guiding the robot in your home at agreed times. Buyers should read 1X's privacy terms before ordering. Figure, for comparison, says its Helix model learned from about 500 hours of remotely operated demonstrations; see VLA models explained.

Built for a home. 1X says NEO's hardware is wrapped in a custom 3D lattice polymer for cushioning, its joints are covered so the surface is pinch-proof, and its suit and shoes are machine-washable nylon. It uses what 1X calls Tendon Drive actuation for precise, low-energy movement,.
How it compares. NEO is one of only a few humanoids with a public price; see our price comparison. Its published runtime is in published humanoid runtimes.
analysis: Analysis: NEO's model is honest about something most of the industry glosses over: home robots are not yet fully autonomous, so 1X builds remote human help into the product. That makes the robot useful sooner, but it also makes privacy and trust part of what you are buying, not an afterthought.

title: NVIDIA Isaac GR00T explained: the open models and tools behind many humanoids
seo_title: NVIDIA Isaac GR00T explained
summary: GR00T is NVIDIA's family of open humanoid robot foundation models plus simulation and data tools. GR00T N1 launched in March 2025; NVIDIA now lists GR00T 1.7.
body: Short answer: Isaac GR00T is NVIDIA's platform for humanoid robot developers: a family of open foundation models that turn instructions and camera input into robot actions, plus tools for collecting data, training in simulation and running the result on NVIDIA's Jetson Thor computer. NVIDIA announced GR00T N1, which it called the world's first open humanoid robot foundation model, on 18 March 2025. Its developer page now lists GR00T 1.7 as the latest open vision-language-action model in the family.

How the model works. NVIDIA said GR00T N1 uses a dual-system design. "System 2" is a slower vision-language model that reasons about the scene and the instruction and plans actions. "System 1" is a fast action model that turns the plan into precise, continuous movements, and NVIDIA said it was trained on human demonstration data and a large amount of synthetic data. Figure's Helix uses a similar split; see what is a VLA model.

GR00T 1.7. According to NVIDIA's developer page, GR00T 1.7 is a 3-billion-parameter model with a Cosmos backend and a commercial licence, available on GitHub, Hugging Face and the LeRobot library. NVIDIA says it can run on Jetson Thor at 25 Hz using TensorRT with NVFP4 quantisation.

The workflow. NVIDIA describes three steps: capture demonstrations by teleoperation in simulation or on a real robot; post-train GR00T on real or simulated demonstrations and evaluate in Isaac Lab-Arena; then deploy the trained policy on Jetson Thor for on-robot inference. It also offers a GR00T-Ready evaluation for robot makers and a Halos safety offering for humanoids.

Why it matters. Because the models are open, smaller robot makers and labs can start from a pre-trained base instead of training from scratch. Many companies in our coverage build on NVIDIA hardware or software; see the NVIDIA hub and our report on NVIDIA's Agile ONE SN reference humanoid.
